1	# Session Context — ResearchGPT Major Project
2	
3	> **What this file is.** A complete record of the planning session held on **2026-08-06**: every constraint established, every decision made and why, every document produced, every finding that changes the build, and everything still open.
4	>
5	> **Read this first** if you are resuming work, handing over to a teammate, or starting a fresh session. It replaces having to re-read the whole conversation.
6	>
7	> **Status at end of session: no code has been written.** Implementation is at Day 0. Everything below is planning, literature, and design artefacts.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## 1. Project identity
12	
13	| | |
14	|---|---|
15	| **Title** | A Multi-Agent Agentic RAG Platform for Automated Literature Review |
16	| **Internal name** | ResearchGPT |
17	| **Institution** | Gokaraju Rangaraju Institute of Engineering and Technology (Autonomous), Dept. of Data Science |
18	| **Course** | IV Year B.Tech, I Semester — CSE (Data Science) |
19	| **Batch** | DSC06 |
20	| **Team** | Abrarullah Mohammed (23241A67D1) · G. Shashivadan Rao (23241A67F2) · P. Sreekaran Reddy (23241A67H7) |
21	| **Guide** | Dr. S. Govinda Rao, Head of Department, Data Science |
22	| **Reviews** | Review-1 completed (`Review-1 dsc06.pptx`) |
23	| **Deadline** | ~30 days from 2026-08-06 → target submission **~2026-09-05** |
24	
25	### The three objectives (PPT slide 5 — exactly three, count is correct)
26	
27	1. Automate end-to-end literature review using a multi-agent agentic RAG pipeline.
28	2. Ensure factual grounding and coverage completeness via verification and critique loops **and Human-in-the-loop**.
29	3. Deliver a usable full-stack application with real-time progress visibility.
30	
31	---
32	
33	## 2. The five constraints that drive every decision
34	
35	These were established during the session and override the original spec wherever they conflict.
36	
37	| # | Constraint | Consequence |
38	|---|---|---|
39	| 1 | **Zero API budget.** No paid services at all. | Free-tier LLM only; everything high-volume moved to local CPU. |
40	| 2 | **CPU-only development machine.** No GPU. | All local models resized for CPU. Ollama demoted to non-viable. Training happens on free Kaggle GPU only. |
41	| 3 | **A model-training component is required** (even a small one). | NLI claim verifier fine-tuned on SciFact — see §4. |
42	| 4 | **Grading is weighted to the system working and not hallucinating**, not to paper polish. | Verifier is the centrepiece. Demo outranks the ablation table. Descope ladder reversed. |
43	| 5 | **Vue.js frontend mandatory**; backend free choice. | Streamlit dropped, FastAPI restored, REST + SSE. |
44	
45	---
46	
47	## 3. Architecture as settled
48	
49	Six agents in a LangGraph state machine with a bounded critic loop. **The design was reviewed against the literature and found sound — no structural change needed.** What changed is the surrounding stack and the diagrams.
50	
51	```
52	Vue 3 SPA  ──REST──▶  FastAPI  ──▶  LangGraph StateGraph
53	    ▲                                      │
54	    └──────────── SSE progress ────────────┤
55	                                           ▼
56	   PLANNER → RETRIEVER → INGEST → RANK → EXTRACTOR
57	                                           │
58	                                           ▼
59	   VERIFIER → (NLI classify) → CRITIC → HUMAN-IN-THE-LOOP
60	                  │                │
61	                  │                ├─ RETRIEVE (coverage gap) ─┐
62	                  │                ├─ REPLAN (plan flawed) ────┤ max 3 iterations
63	                  │                └─ WRITE ───────────────────┘
64	                                           ▼
65	                                        WRITER → artefacts → Vue
66	```
67	
68	**Where each part runs** — this is the key to the $0 constraint working:
69	
70	| Function | Location | Cost |
71	|---|---|---|
72	| Embeddings (`bge-small-en-v1.5`, ~33M) | Local CPU | $0, unlimited |
73	| Reranking (`ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2`, ~22M) | Local CPU | $0, unlimited |
74	| **Claim verification (fine-tuned NLI, ONNX int8)** | **Local CPU** | **$0, unlimited** |
75	| Planner, Extractor, Critic, Writer | Free-tier hosted LLM | $0, rate-limited |
76	| Model training | Kaggle GPU (~30 h/week free) | $0 |
77	
78	Only four generative calls per run consume the scarce resource, and only the Extractor scales with paper count (~70 calls per run).
79	
80	---
81	
82	## 4. Major decisions and the reasoning
83	
84	### 4.1 Training target: the claim verifier, not the reranker ⬅ changed mid-session
85	
86	Originally proposed fine-tuning the cross-encoder reranker on SciReviewGen. **Switched to a claim verifier** for three reasons:
87	
88	- It sits on the graded critical path — you're graded on hallucination; the verifier *is* the anti-hallucination mechanism.
89	- **No access lead time.** SciFact downloads straight from Hugging Face. The reranker route needed S2ORC access, historically a multi-day AI2 request — the single biggest schedule risk.
90	- It removes API load. An LLM verifier costs one call per atomic claim (hundreds per run). A local cross-encoder is free and deterministic.
91	
92	**Recipe:** `deberta-v3-small` (~44M, warm-started from an NLI checkpoint) → 3-way classification `SUPPORT / CONTRADICT / NOT_ENOUGH_INFO` on SciFact → 2–3 epochs on Kaggle, under an hour → **export ONNX int8 for CPU inference**. Softmax probability becomes `support_score`, threshold 0.7.
93	
94	*Escalate to `deberta-v3-base` if held-out F1 is poor. Trade latency, not accuracy — the verifier is the graded component.*
95	
96	### 4.2 LLM: Gemini free tier primary, Groq backup
97	
98	Chosen on **JSON-parse reliability** (the Extractor's 4-field schema must parse) and context window, not benchmark scores. Register both on Day 1 and spend thirty minutes testing the Extractor prompt on each.
99	
100	**Mandatory Day-1 engineering:** prompt-hash **response cache** to disk (the single highest-leverage thing in the build — dev re-runs then cost zero requests), exponential backoff on 429s, requests-per-minute throttle, and a rate-limit guardrail replacing the spec's `max_cost_usd`.
101	
102	### 4.3 Stack decisions vs. the original spec
103	
104	| Item | Spec said | Now | Why |
105	|---|---|---|---|
106	| Vector store | Chroma → Qdrant | **Chroma, no migration** | ~3k vectors; Qdrant unjustified |
107	| Sources | 10 connectors | **OpenAlex + arXiv** | Crossref redundant; **Semantic Scholar hit HTTP 429 during this session** |
108	| PDF parsing | PyMuPDF + GROBID | **PyMuPDF only** | GROBID is a Docker service for marginal gain |
109	| Frontend | Streamlit (optional) | **Vue 3 + Vite, no Pinia** | Mandated; one page, one run — a store is ceremony |
110	| Backend | FastAPI (cut, then restored) | **FastAPI + REST + SSE** | Needed as the Vue backend |
111	| Determinism | vcrpy cassettes | **JSON response cache** | ~20 lines, and doubles as rate-limit protection |
112	| RAGAs | Full framework | **Cut the library, keep the metric** | `F = |V|/|S|` is computable free from verifier output |
113	| Ablations | 7 | **4** | Rate limits make each run expensive in wall clock |
114	| Human eval | 3 annotators, Krippendorff α | **2 annotators, Cohen κ** | Scheduling problem, not technical |
115	
116	### 4.4 Base paper: switch recommended ⚠️
117	
118	See §5.1 — this is the most consequential finding of the session.
119	
120	---
121	
122	## 5. Critical findings
123	
124	### 5.1 ⚠️ The base paper is not what the spec says it is
125	
126	`RESEARCHGPT_SPEC.md §1.2` describes Aytar et al. (2025) as *"RAG-based literature assistance."*
127	
128	**The paper is real and correctly attributed** — DOI [10.1016/j.nlp.2025.100179](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nlp.2025.100179), *Natural Language Processing Journal* (Elsevier, Scopus) — but its actual title is **"A synergistic multi-stage RAG architecture for boosting context relevance in data science literature."** It optimises retrieval precision in the data-science domain. It does not generate literature reviews.
129	
130	Two consequences:
131	
132	1. **`§1.3`'s extension table contains a factual error.** It claims the base paper uses a *"fixed single-pass pipeline."* It is explicitly **multi-stage** (GROBID parsing, fine-tuned embeddings, semantic chunking, abstract-first retrieval). That row is the foundation of the "we are more agentic" argument. **Rewrite it** — the honest contrast is *static multi-stage vs. dynamic agentic control with verification*.
133	2. **It also uses GROBID**, which the plan cuts. If Aytar stays as base paper, dropping GROBID becomes a deviation to defend.
134	
135	**Recommendation: switch the base paper to SurveyGen** (Bao et al., EMNLP 2025, DOI `10.18653/v1/2025.emnlp-main.136`). Same task, RAG pipeline with quality-aware retrieval that maps onto your venue tiering, and — decisively — their own stated conclusion is your problem statement:
136	
137	> *"Fully automatic survey generation still suffers from low citation quality and limited critical analysis."*
138	
139	Low citation quality → your Verifier. Limited critical analysis → your four-field schema. You cite the base paper's authors describing the gap rather than asserting it yourself. Second choice: **Valsci** (BMC Bioinformatics 2025), SciFact-evaluated like your verifier.
140	
141	### 5.2 Calibration numbers — revise your targets before building
142	
143	`PROJECT_PLAN.md §9` currently targets groundedness ≥ 0.9. Nothing in the peer-reviewed literature reaches that on realistic scientific verification:
144	
145	| Source | Measurement |
146	|---|---|
147	| **Sarol et al. 2024** (essentially your Verifier: BM25 + MonoT5 + fine-tuned MultiVerS) | **0.59 micro-F1** on real citations |
148	| **CliVER 2024** | **0.93** Oracle → **0.85** Open retrieval → **0.797** vs clinicians → **0.44** worst domain |
149	| **SurveyGen 2025** | Best citation accuracy **35.84%**; QUAL-SG citation-quality F1 **16.73%** |
150	| **SciReviewGen 2023** | ~**30%** of generated chapters match human quality |
151	
152	**If your verifier reports 0.9+ against real citations, suspect your measurement, not a breakthrough.**
153	
154	### 5.3 Four independent measurements of the same failure — your Introduction
155	
156	| Source | Finding |
157	|---|---|
158	| Sarol et al. | **39.18%** of citation instances in highly-cited biomedical papers contain accuracy errors (historical median 20%) |
159	| ALCE (Gao et al.) | Best models *"lack complete citation support 50% of the time"* |
160	| FActScore (Min et al.) | ChatGPT factually correct on only **58%** of atomic claims in long-form generation |
161	| SurveyGen | Best survey-generation citation accuracy **35.84%** |
162	
163	### 5.4 The presence of a citation carries almost no information
164	
165	FActScore: **36.0%** of *supported* sentences and **37.6%** of *unsupported* sentences carried citations — statistically indistinguishable. This is the deepest justification for claim-level verification, and it means DOI-resolution checking is necessary but shallow.
166	
167	### 5.5 Architecture beats model scale — measured
168	
169	**Valsci Table 3:** GPT-4o-mini *inside* their architecture scores **F1 0.720**; bare GPT-4o scores **0.706**. A small cheap model plus good architecture beats a frontier model alone. This is published prior support for the project's narrative: *the architecture is a correctness filter, not a correctness source.* Quote it in the Introduction and again in the Discussion — it converts the $0 constraint from an apology into a hypothesis.
170	
171	### 5.6 Your closest competitor names your contribution as its own limitation
172	
173	**Ammann et al. (ACL SRW 2025)** — LLM query decomposition + per-sub-question retrieval + cross-encoder rerank, *"without any extra training"*, reporting +36.7% MRR@10. That is your Planner + Retriever. Their Limitations section, item 6:
174	
175	> *"Lack of iterative retrieval. Our pipeline operates in a single-shot manner: subqueries are generated once and not updated based on retrieved evidence. This limits its ability to support adaptive multi-step reasoning."*
176	
177	That is exactly what your Critic loop does. **Quote it verbatim.** Also treat their numbers as a Day-5 sanity check, and their configuration as a stronger ablation-4 baseline than vanilla RAG.
178	
179	Their limitation #5 is a warning: *"the observed gains rely on a strong, domain-aligned cross-encoder reranker"* — and yours is a 22M MiniLM. Measure reranking's contribution separately.
180	
181	### 5.7 Abstract-only conditioning costs 21 points of faithfulness
182	
183	**Li et al. (SDP@ACL 2024)** measured ANLI faithfulness of generated citations: **Abstract 0.745** vs **Context-CTS 0.959 / Oracle 0.940 / Keyword 0.941**, consistent across two generators. Their conclusion: abstract-conditioned models *"learn to hallucinate."*
184	
185	**This threatens the planned abstract-only degraded mode for paywalled papers.** Recommended fix: abstract-only papers may be **cited as existing but may not supply verified claims**. Note the tension with the base paper's "Abstract First" finding — abstracts may be good for *retrieval* and bad for *grounding*.
186	
187	### 5.8 Humans agree poorly on exactly what you plan to measure
188	
189	| Study | Agreement |
190	|---|---|
191	| Sarol et al. | κ **0.18–0.31** (accuracy labels) |
192	| CiteBench | κ **0.18–0.42** (consistency) |
193	| SciReviewGen | κ **0.212** (three-way review quality) |
194	| CliVER | Fleiss κ 0.684 (own curated claims) |
195	
196	Consequences: use **two annotators and report κ**; a verifier at 0.59 against humans agreeing 0.3 is not obviously failing; prefer objective metrics as primary evidence.
197	
198	### 5.9 SciReviewGen's limitations list is a requirements document for your system
199	
200	| Their stated limitation | Your response |
201	|---|---|
202	| Only abstracts as input | Full-text parsing + `evidence_spans` |
203	| Chapters generated independently | Writer synthesises across themes; Critic assesses globally |
204	| Inter-paper relations ignored | Thematic clustering + `contradiction_pairs` |
205	| Output contains incorrect information | Verifier removes unsupported claims |
206	
207	### 5.10 Smaller actionable findings
208	
209	- **Dagdelen et al.**: structured output stabilises at **~20 few-shot examples**; below ~10 it is malformed. Sets your Extractor prompt. Also — schema format interacts with model (JSON best for Llama-2, English-sentence for GPT-3), so A/B it.
210	- **CliVER**: **21% false-Support rate** (recall 1.0, precision 0.79). Over-predicting "supported" is the dangerous direction for a hallucination-graded project. Weight the `SUPPORTED` threshold toward precision.
211	- **ALCE**: post-hoc citation attachment cost **47% of citation recall**. Validates the evidence-first Writer constraint.
212	- **Retrieval recall is a hard ceiling** on verification — stated independently by ALCE, Sarol (top-20 recall 0.53) and Valsci. Protect the Day 6–7 retrieval buffer.
213	- **Bolaños et al.**: use **F2 not F1** for screening (recall matters more than precision when discarding papers).
214	- **CiteBench**: ROUGE package configuration alone swings scores ~3 points — specify yours.
215	- **FActScore scope limit**: its method *"is not applicable when the facts are more nuanced, open-ended, and debatable."* Your `disadvantages` and `critique` fields are exactly that — consider verifying only the objective fields strictly.
216	
217	---
218	
219	## 6. Documents produced this session
220	
221	All in `C:\Users\Sreekaran\Desktop\Major Project\`.
222	
223	| File | Contents |
224	|---|---|
225	| **`PROJECT_PLAN.md`** | 30-day execution plan. Scope cuts with rationale, $0/CPU model strategy, day-by-day timeline, evaluation design, **descope ladder**, risk table. Revised three times as constraints emerged. |
226	| **`LITERATURE_REVIEW.md`** | 25 papers (2023–2026, peer-reviewed), comparative table across Problem/Methodology/Advantages/Disadvantages/Datasets/DOI, thematic synthesis, gaps, **3 ranked base-paper candidates**, verification report, 9-paper reserve pool. |
227	| **`PAPER_ANALYSIS.md`** | Per-paper extensive analysis (6 fields + relevance) written from verified abstracts. |
228	| **`PAPER_DEEP_DIVE.md`** | Full-text deep dive. **18 of 26 papers obtained in full text**; 8 abstract-only and marked as such. Every reported number, verbatim limitations, cross-cutting synthesis, 14 ranked actions. |
229	| **`ARCHITECTURE_REVIEW.md`** | Audit of the spec's architecture diagram and MCD against the three review rules. Corrected UML activity diagram, UML component diagram, UML MCD, classical structure chart alternative, PPT consistency table, objective refinements. |
230	| **`diagrams/01_architecture_diagram.drawio`** | UML 2.5 activity diagram, 3 swimlane partitions (one per objective), 33 vertices / 32 edges. |
231	| **`diagrams/02_module_connectivity_diagram.drawio`** | UML 2.5 component diagram, 4 `«subsystem»` packages, 27 vertices / 29 edges. |
232	| **`SESSION_CONTEXT.md`** | This file. |
233	
234	Pre-existing: `RESEARCHGPT_SPEC.md`, `Review-1 dsc06.pptx`, `Literature papers/` (7 PDFs).
235	
236	---
237	
238	## 7. Corrections required to existing documents
239	
240	### 7.1 `RESEARCHGPT_SPEC.md`
241	
242	| Section | Fix |
243	|---|---|
244	| §1.2 | Base paper mis-described. Correct the title/scope, or switch to SurveyGen. |
245	| §1.3 | *"Fixed single-pass pipeline"* is factually wrong — Aytar et al. is multi-stage. |
246	| §3 | Architecture diagram: not UML, no input/output zones, **Objective 3 absent entirely** (no Vue/FastAPI), **HITL absent**. Replace with the draw.io file. |
247	| §4 | Package-dependency graph, not an MCD. Keep it but relabel "Package Dependency Map" and add the real MCD. |
248	| §7.5 | Add human-in-the-loop to the Critic. |

250	
251	### 7.2 `Review-1 dsc06.pptx`
252	
253	| Slide | Problem | Severity |
254	|---|---|---|
255	| 6 | *"GPU: 8GB Minimum"* — machine is CPU-only. Specifies hardware you don't have. | ⚠️ **Visible error** |
256	| 8 | *"Extractor chunks and embeds them"* — that's the Ingestor's job. As written, the system has **no structured extraction**, deleting a main contribution. | ⚠️ **Visible error** |
257	| 3, 8, 9 | pgvector/PostgreSQL vs Chroma everywhere else. Chroma avoids running Postgres + Docker. | Medium |
258	| 3, 6 | Semantic Scholar as a source — rate-limited without a key (confirmed 429 this session). | Medium |
259	| 7 | Replace architecture diagram. | High |

261	| 11 | Processing-branch sentence needs the 2.1 / 2.2 split. | Medium |
262	| 12 | ○/● couple explanation only applies to the structure-chart version — rewrite if going UML. | Medium |
263	| 5 | Objectives: lowercase "to automate/ensure/deliver"; **add the trained verifier to Objective 2** so there's an answer to "where's the ML?" | Low but valuable |
264	
265	---
266	
267	## 8. Open items — only you can close these
268	
269	1. **Get the PDF of Li et al., *Information Processing & Management*** (DOI `10.1016/j.ipm.2025.104369`) through your library. ScienceDirect returns HTTP 403 to automated access, so it is the one paper in the set written from its title alone. "Evidence-aware" + "self-corrective" describes your Verifier and Critic — **it may be a competitor to differentiate from, not a supporting citation.** Also: OpenAlex dates it 2025, Semantic Scholar 2026 — resolve before it enters your reference list.
270	2. **Confirm the base-paper switch with your guide** (Aytar → SurveyGen).
271	3. **Confirm which MCD notation the rubric means** — UML component diagram, or classical Yourdon/Constantine structure chart. Both are prepared; they need different slide 12 text.

# Session Context — ResearchGPT Major Project

> **What this file is.** A complete record of the planning session held on **2026-08-06**: every constraint established, every decision made and why, every document produced, every finding that changes the build, and everything still open.
>
> **Read this first** if you are resuming work, handing over to a teammate, or starting a fresh session. It replaces having to re-read the whole conversation.
>
> **Status at end of session: no code has been written.** Implementation is at Day 0. Everything below is planning, literature, and design artefacts.

---

## 1. Project identity

| | |
|---|---|
| **Title** | A Multi-Agent Agentic RAG Platform for Automated Literature Review |
| **Internal name** | ResearchGPT |
| **Institution** | Gokaraju Rangaraju Institute of Engineering and Technology (Autonomous), Dept. of Data Science |
| **Course** | IV Year B.Tech, I Semester — CSE (Data Science) |
| **Batch** | DSC06 |
| **Team** | Abrarullah Mohammed (23241A67D1) · G. Shashivadan Rao (23241A67F2) · P. Sreekaran Reddy (23241A67H7) |
| **Guide** | Dr. S. Govinda Rao, Head of Department, Data Science |
| **Reviews** | Review-1 completed (`Review-1 dsc06.pptx`) |
| **Deadline** | ~30 days from 2026-08-06 → target submission **~2026-09-05** |

### The three objectives (PPT slide 5 — exactly three, count is correct)

1. Automate end-to-end literature review using a multi-agent agentic RAG pipeline.
2. Ensure factual grounding and coverage completeness via verification and critique loops **and Human-in-the-loop**.
3. Deliver a usable full-stack application with real-time progress visibility.

---

## 2. The five constraints that drive every decision

These were established during the session and override the original spec wherever they conflict.

| # | Constraint | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Zero API budget.** No paid services at all. | Free-tier LLM only; everything high-volume moved to local CPU. |
| 2 | **CPU-only development machine.** No GPU. | All local models resized for CPU. Ollama demoted to non-viable. Training happens on free Kaggle GPU only. |
| 3 | **A model-training component is required** (even a small one). | NLI claim verifier fine-tuned on SciFact — see §4. |
| 4 | **Grading is weighted to the system working and not hallucinating**, not to paper polish. | Verifier is the centrepiece. Demo outranks the ablation table. Descope ladder reversed. |
| 5 | **Vue.js frontend mandatory**; backend free choice. | Streamlit dropped, FastAPI restored, REST + SSE. |

---

## 3. Architecture as settled

Six agents in a LangGraph state machine with a bounded critic loop. **The design was reviewed against the literature and found sound — no structural change needed.** What changed is the surrounding stack and the diagrams.

```
Vue 3 SPA  ──REST──▶  FastAPI  ──▶  LangGraph StateGraph
    ▲                                      │
    └──────────── SSE progress ────────────┤
                                           ▼
   PLANNER → RETRIEVER → INGEST → RANK → EXTRACTOR
                                           │
                                           ▼
   VERIFIER → (NLI classify) → CRITIC → HUMAN-IN-THE-LOOP
                  │                │
                  │                ├─ RETRIEVE (coverage gap) ─┐
                  │                ├─ REPLAN (plan flawed) ────┤ max 3 iterations
                  │                └─ WRITE ───────────────────┘
                                           ▼
                                        WRITER → artefacts → Vue
```

**Where each part runs** — this is the key to the $0 constraint working:

| Function | Location | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Embeddings (`bge-small-en-v1.5`, ~33M) | Local CPU | $0, unlimited |
| Reranking (`ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2`, ~22M) | Local CPU | $0, unlimited |
| **Claim verification (fine-tuned NLI, ONNX int8)** | **Local CPU** | **$0, unlimited** |
| Planner, Extractor, Critic, Writer | Free-tier hosted LLM | $0, rate-limited |
| Model training | Kaggle GPU (~30 h/week free) | $0 |

Only four generative calls per run consume the scarce resource, and only the Extractor scales with paper count (~70 calls per run).

---

## 4. Major decisions and the reasoning

### 4.1 Training target: the claim verifier, not the reranker ⬅ changed mid-session

Originally proposed fine-tuning the cross-encoder reranker on SciReviewGen. **Switched to a claim verifier** for three reasons:

- It sits on the graded critical path — you're graded on hallucination; the verifier *is* the anti-hallucination mechanism.
- **No access lead time.** SciFact downloads straight from Hugging Face. The reranker route needed S2ORC access, historically a multi-day AI2 request — the single biggest schedule risk.
- It removes API load. An LLM verifier costs one call per atomic claim (hundreds per run). A local cross-encoder is free and deterministic.

**Recipe:** `deberta-v3-small` (~44M, warm-started from an NLI checkpoint) → 3-way classification `SUPPORT / CONTRADICT / NOT_ENOUGH_INFO` on SciFact → 2–3 epochs on Kaggle, under an hour → **export ONNX int8 for CPU inference**. Softmax probability becomes `support_score`, threshold 0.7.

*Escalate to `deberta-v3-base` if held-out F1 is poor. Trade latency, not accuracy — the verifier is the graded component.*

### 4.2 LLM: Gemini free tier primary, Groq backup

Chosen on **JSON-parse reliability** (the Extractor's 4-field schema must parse) and context window, not benchmark scores. Register both on Day 1 and spend thirty minutes testing the Extractor prompt on each.

**Mandatory Day-1 engineering:** prompt-hash **response cache** to disk (the single highest-leverage thing in the build — dev re-runs then cost zero requests), exponential backoff on 429s, requests-per-minute throttle, and a rate-limit guardrail replacing the spec's `max_cost_usd`.

### 4.3 Stack decisions vs. the original spec

| Item | Spec said | Now | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vector store | Chroma → Qdrant | **Chroma, no migration** | ~3k vectors; Qdrant unjustified |
| Sources | 10 connectors | **OpenAlex + arXiv** | Crossref redundant; **Semantic Scholar hit HTTP 429 during this session** |
| PDF parsing | PyMuPDF + GROBID | **PyMuPDF only** | GROBID is a Docker service for marginal gain |
| Frontend | Streamlit (optional) | **Vue 3 + Vite, no Pinia** | Mandated; one page, one run — a store is ceremony |
| Backend | FastAPI (cut, then restored) | **FastAPI + REST + SSE** | Needed as the Vue backend |
| Determinism | vcrpy cassettes | **JSON response cache** | ~20 lines, and doubles as rate-limit protection |
| RAGAs | Full framework | **Cut the library, keep the metric** | `F = |V|/|S|` is computable free from verifier output |
| Ablations | 7 | **4** | Rate limits make each run expensive in wall clock |
| Human eval | 3 annotators, Krippendorff α | **2 annotators, Cohen κ** | Scheduling problem, not technical |

### 4.4 Base paper: switch recommended ⚠️

See §5.1 — this is the most consequential finding of the session.

---

## 5. Critical findings

### 5.1 ⚠️ The base paper is not what the spec says it is

`RESEARCHGPT_SPEC.md §1.2` describes Aytar et al. (2025) as *"RAG-based literature assistance."*

**The paper is real and correctly attributed** — DOI [10.1016/j.nlp.2025.100179](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nlp.2025.100179), *Natural Language Processing Journal* (Elsevier, Scopus) — but its actual title is **"A synergistic multi-stage RAG architecture for boosting context relevance in data science literature."** It optimises retrieval precision in the data-science domain. It does not generate literature reviews.

Two consequences:

1. **`§1.3`'s extension table contains a factual error.** It claims the base paper uses a *"fixed single-pass pipeline."* It is explicitly **multi-stage** (GROBID parsing, fine-tuned embeddings, semantic chunking, abstract-first retrieval). That row is the foundation of the "we are more agentic" argument. **Rewrite it** — the honest contrast is *static multi-stage vs. dynamic agentic control with verification*.
2. **It also uses GROBID**, which the plan cuts. If Aytar stays as base paper, dropping GROBID becomes a deviation to defend.

**Recommendation: switch the base paper to SurveyGen** (Bao et al., EMNLP 2025, DOI `10.18653/v1/2025.emnlp-main.136`). Same task, RAG pipeline with quality-aware retrieval that maps onto your venue tiering, and — decisively — their own stated conclusion is your problem statement:

> *"Fully automatic survey generation still suffers from low citation quality and limited critical analysis."*

Low citation quality → your Verifier. Limited critical analysis → your four-field schema. You cite the base paper's authors describing the gap rather than asserting it yourself. Second choice: **Valsci** (BMC Bioinformatics 2025), SciFact-evaluated like your verifier.

### 5.2 Calibration numbers — revise your targets before building

`PROJECT_PLAN.md §9` currently targets groundedness ≥ 0.9. Nothing in the peer-reviewed literature reaches that on realistic scientific verification:

| Source | Measurement |
|---|---|
| **Sarol et al. 2024** (essentially your Verifier: BM25 + MonoT5 + fine-tuned MultiVerS) | **0.59 micro-F1** on real citations |
| **CliVER 2024** | **0.93** Oracle → **0.85** Open retrieval → **0.797** vs clinicians → **0.44** worst domain |
| **SurveyGen 2025** | Best citation accuracy **35.84%**; QUAL-SG citation-quality F1 **16.73%** |
| **SciReviewGen 2023** | ~**30%** of generated chapters match human quality |

**If your verifier reports 0.9+ against real citations, suspect your measurement, not a breakthrough.**

### 5.3 Four independent measurements of the same failure — your Introduction

| Source | Finding |
|---|---|
| Sarol et al. | **39.18%** of citation instances in highly-cited biomedical papers contain accuracy errors (historical median 20%) |
| ALCE (Gao et al.) | Best models *"lack complete citation support 50% of the time"* |
| FActScore (Min et al.) | ChatGPT factually correct on only **58%** of atomic claims in long-form generation |
| SurveyGen | Best survey-generation citation accuracy **35.84%** |

### 5.4 The presence of a citation carries almost no information

FActScore: **36.0%** of *supported* sentences and **37.6%** of *unsupported* sentences carried citations — statistically indistinguishable. This is the deepest justification for claim-level verification, and it means DOI-resolution checking is necessary but shallow.

### 5.5 Architecture beats model scale — measured

**Valsci Table 3:** GPT-4o-mini *inside* their architecture scores **F1 0.720**; bare GPT-4o scores **0.706**. A small cheap model plus good architecture beats a frontier model alone. This is published prior support for the project's narrative: *the architecture is a correctness filter, not a correctness source.* Quote it in the Introduction and again in the Discussion — it converts the $0 constraint from an apology into a hypothesis.

### 5.6 Your closest competitor names your contribution as its own limitation

**Ammann et al. (ACL SRW 2025)** — LLM query decomposition + per-sub-question retrieval + cross-encoder rerank, *"without any extra training"*, reporting +36.7% MRR@10. That is your Planner + Retriever. Their Limitations section, item 6:

> *"Lack of iterative retrieval. Our pipeline operates in a single-shot manner: subqueries are generated once and not updated based on retrieved evidence. This limits its ability to support adaptive multi-step reasoning."*

That is exactly what your Critic loop does. **Quote it verbatim.** Also treat their numbers as a Day-5 sanity check, and their configuration as a stronger ablation-4 baseline than vanilla RAG.

Their limitation #5 is a warning: *"the observed gains rely on a strong, domain-aligned cross-encoder reranker"* — and yours is a 22M MiniLM. Measure reranking's contribution separately.

### 5.7 Abstract-only conditioning costs 21 points of faithfulness

**Li et al. (SDP@ACL 2024)** measured ANLI faithfulness of generated citations: **Abstract 0.745** vs **Context-CTS 0.959 / Oracle 0.940 / Keyword 0.941**, consistent across two generators. Their conclusion: abstract-conditioned models *"learn to hallucinate."*

**This threatens the planned abstract-only degraded mode for paywalled papers.** Recommended fix: abstract-only papers may be **cited as existing but may not supply verified claims**. Note the tension with the base paper's "Abstract First" finding — abstracts may be good for *retrieval* and bad for *grounding*.

### 5.8 Humans agree poorly on exactly what you plan to measure

| Study | Agreement |
|---|---|
| Sarol et al. | κ **0.18–0.31** (accuracy labels) |
| CiteBench | κ **0.18–0.42** (consistency) |
| SciReviewGen | κ **0.212** (three-way review quality) |
| CliVER | Fleiss κ 0.684 (own curated claims) |

Consequences: use **two annotators and report κ**; a verifier at 0.59 against humans agreeing 0.3 is not obviously failing; prefer objective metrics as primary evidence.

### 5.9 SciReviewGen's limitations list is a requirements document for your system

| Their stated limitation | Your response |
|---|---|
| Only abstracts as input | Full-text parsing + `evidence_spans` |
| Chapters generated independently | Writer synthesises across themes; Critic assesses globally |
| Inter-paper relations ignored | Thematic clustering + `contradiction_pairs` |
| Output contains incorrect information | Verifier removes unsupported claims |

### 5.10 Smaller actionable findings

- **Dagdelen et al.**: structured output stabilises at **~20 few-shot examples**; below ~10 it is malformed. Sets your Extractor prompt. Also — schema format interacts with model (JSON best for Llama-2, English-sentence for GPT-3), so A/B it.
- **CliVER**: **21% false-Support rate** (recall 1.0, precision 0.79). Over-predicting "supported" is the dangerous direction for a hallucination-graded project. Weight the `SUPPORTED` threshold toward precision.
- **ALCE**: post-hoc citation attachment cost **47% of citation recall**. Validates the evidence-first Writer constraint.
- **Retrieval recall is a hard ceiling** on verification — stated independently by ALCE, Sarol (top-20 recall 0.53) and Valsci. Protect the Day 6–7 retrieval buffer.
- **Bolaños et al.**: use **F2 not F1** for screening (recall matters more than precision when discarding papers).
- **CiteBench**: ROUGE package configuration alone swings scores ~3 points — specify yours.
- **FActScore scope limit**: its method *"is not applicable when the facts are more nuanced, open-ended, and debatable."* Your `disadvantages` and `critique` fields are exactly that — consider verifying only the objective fields strictly.

---

## 6. Documents produced this session

All in `C:\Users\Sreekaran\Desktop\Major Project\`.

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| **`PROJECT_PLAN.md`** | 30-day execution plan. Scope cuts with rationale, $0/CPU model strategy, day-by-day timeline, evaluation design, **descope ladder**, risk table. Revised three times as constraints emerged. |
| **`LITERATURE_REVIEW.md`** | 25 papers (2023–2026, peer-reviewed), comparative table across Problem/Methodology/Advantages/Disadvantages/Datasets/DOI, thematic synthesis, gaps, **3 ranked base-paper candidates**, verification report, 9-paper reserve pool. |
| **`PAPER_ANALYSIS.md`** | Per-paper extensive analysis (6 fields + relevance) written from verified abstracts. |
| **`PAPER_DEEP_DIVE.md`** | Full-text deep dive. **18 of 26 papers obtained in full text**; 8 abstract-only and marked as such. Every reported number, verbatim limitations, cross-cutting synthesis, 14 ranked actions. |
| **`ARCHITECTURE_REVIEW.md`** | Audit of the spec's architecture diagram and MCD against the three review rules. Corrected UML activity diagram, UML component diagram, UML MCD, classical structure chart alternative, PPT consistency table, objective refinements. |
| **`diagrams/01_architecture_diagram.drawio`** | UML 2.5 activity diagram, 3 swimlane partitions (one per objective), 33 vertices / 32 edges. |
| **`diagrams/02_module_connectivity_diagram.drawio`** | UML 2.5 component diagram, 4 `«subsystem»` packages, 27 vertices / 29 edges. |
| **`SESSION_CONTEXT.md`** | This file. |

Pre-existing: `RESEARCHGPT_SPEC.md`, `Review-1 dsc06.pptx`, `Literature papers/` (7 PDFs).

---

## 7. Corrections required to existing documents

### 7.1 `RESEARCHGPT_SPEC.md`

| Section | Fix |
|---|---|
| §1.2 | Base paper mis-described. Correct the title/scope, or switch to SurveyGen. |
| §1.3 | *"Fixed single-pass pipeline"* is factually wrong — Aytar et al. is multi-stage. |
| §3 | Architecture diagram: not UML, no input/output zones, **Objective 3 absent entirely** (no Vue/FastAPI), **HITL absent**. Replace with the draw.io file. |
| §4 | Package-dependency graph, not an MCD. Keep it but relabel "Package Dependency Map" and add the real MCD. |
| §7.5 | Add human-in-the-loop to the Critic. |
| §9 | Targets need revising downward per §5.2. |

### 7.2 `Review-1 dsc06.pptx`

| Slide | Problem | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | *"GPU: 8GB Minimum"* — machine is CPU-only. Specifies hardware you don't have. | ⚠️ **Visible error** |
| 8 | *"Extractor chunks and embeds them"* — that's the Ingestor's job. As written, the system has **no structured extraction**, deleting a main contribution. | ⚠️ **Visible error** |
| 3, 8, 9 | pgvector/PostgreSQL vs Chroma everywhere else. Chroma avoids running Postgres + Docker. | Medium |
| 3, 6 | Semantic Scholar as a source — rate-limited without a key (confirmed 429 this session). | Medium |
| 7 | Replace architecture diagram. | High |
| 10 | Replace MCD. | High |
| 11 | Processing-branch sentence needs the 2.1 / 2.2 split. | Medium |
| 12 | ○/● couple explanation only applies to the structure-chart version — rewrite if going UML. | Medium |
| 5 | Objectives: lowercase "to automate/ensure/deliver"; **add the trained verifier to Objective 2** so there's an answer to "where's the ML?" | Low but valuable |

---

## 8. Open items — only you can close these

1. **Get the PDF of Li et al., *Information Processing & Management*** (DOI `10.1016/j.ipm.2025.104369`) through your library. ScienceDirect returns HTTP 403 to automated access, so it is the one paper in the set written from its title alone. "Evidence-aware" + "self-corrective" describes your Verifier and Critic — **it may be a competitor to differentiate from, not a supporting citation.** Also: OpenAlex dates it 2025, Semantic Scholar 2026 — resolve before it enters your reference list.
2. **Confirm the base-paper switch with your guide** (Aytar → SurveyGen).
3. **Confirm which MCD notation the rubric means** — UML component diagram, or classical Yourdon/Constantine structure chart. Both are prepared; they need different slide 12 text.
4. **Verify *Vicinagearth* is Scopus-indexed** (paper C3-11, launched 2024). If not, substitute Wang et al. 2024, *Frontiers of Computer Science*, DOI `10.1007/s11704-024-40231-1` (1,320 citations).
5. **Decide whether Human-in-the-loop stays in Objective 2.** Keep it only if you build it — the cheapest honest version is the dropped-claims panel with confirm/override, ~half a day on top of the Vue panel already planned.
6. **File the S2ORC access request** if you want SciReviewGen gold sets (nothing critical depends on it now).

Plain `search=` sorted by citations returned irrelevant high-citation medical papers; the strict title/abstract filter fixed it.

# PPTX creation, editing, and analysis

A `.pptx` is a ZIP archive of XML files. Choose your approach by task:

| Task | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Create** a new deck | Write a `pptxgenjs` script — see gotchas below |
| **Edit** an existing deck, or build from a template | unzip → edit `ppt/slides/slideN.xml` → zip |
| **Read** content | `markitdown deck.pptx` (one block per slide under `<!-- Slide number: N -->` markers); visual grid: `python scripts/thumbnail.py deck.pptx` |

## Scripts

Paths are relative to this skill's directory. Everything else is plain Python, `node`, or shell.

| Script | What it does |
|---|---|
| `scripts/thumbnail.py deck.pptx [prefix]` | Labeled grid of every slide, for picking template layouts. `.pptx` only. Pass `prefix` — it defaults to `thumbnails`, which overwrites the grids of any other deck done in the same directory |
| `scripts/add_slide.py unpacked/ slide2.xml [--after slideN.xml]` | Duplicate a slide (or a `slideLayoutN.xml`) with all the package bookkeeping. Also takes a `.pptx` directly with `-o out.pptx` |
| `scripts/clean.py unpacked/` | Delete slides, media, and rels no longer referenced. Run **after** `<p:sldIdLst>` is final |
| `scripts/office/validate.py deck.pptx [--original src.pptx]` | Schema, relationship, content-type, chart and slide checks; each failure names its fix. Pass `--original` for any template-derived deck — it baselines the schema checks against the template, so the template's own XSD errors don't read as yours |
| `scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf deck.pptx` | LibreOffice wrapper — bare `soffice` hangs in this sandbox |

## Creating with pptxgenjs — gotchas

`pptxgenjs` is preinstalled — do not run `npm install` first; write the script and `require('pptxgenjs')` directly. Only if that require fails: `npm install pptxgenjs`. The model knows the API; these are the footguns:

- **Set `pres.layout` before adding slides.** The default canvas is `LAYOUT_16x9` = **10" × 5.625"**, not 13.3" wide. Coordinates past the edge are written, not clamped — the shape just isn't on the slide. (`LAYOUT_WIDE` is 13.3" × 7.5".)
- **Hex colors: never `#`, never 8 digits.** `color: "FF0000"`. Both `"#FF0000"` and alpha baked into the hex (`"00000020"`) **corrupt the file**. For translucency: `transparency: 0-100` on fills and images, `opacity: 0.0-1.0` on shadows — each is silently ignored on the other.
- **pptxgenjs mutates option objects in place** (converts values to EMU on first use). Never share one `shadow`/options object across two `add*` calls — build a fresh object each time.
- **Shadow `offset` must be ≥ 0** — a negative offset corrupts the file. To cast a shadow upward, use `angle: 270` with a positive offset.
- **`letterSpacing` is silently ignored** — the real option is `charSpacing`.
- **Lists:** `bullet: true` on each item, never a literal `•` (renders double bullets). Set `breakLine: true` on every array item except the last. Space bulleted paragraphs with `paraSpaceAfter`, not `lineSpacing` (huge gaps).
- **One `new pptxgen()` per output file** — never reuse an instance.
- **`rectRadius` only works on `ROUNDED_RECTANGLE`**, not `RECTANGLE`.
- **Gradient fills aren't supported** — use a gradient image as the background instead.
- **Text boxes have built-in internal padding** — set `margin: 0` whenever text must align with a shape, line, or icon at the same x.
- **Speaker notes go in `slide.addNotes("...")`** (plain text, once per slide), never in a text box on the slide.
- **Keep charts native.** Use `addChart()` for everything PowerPoint can chart (pass an array of `{type, data, options}` for combos). For PowerPoint-native features the library doesn't expose (trendlines, error bars), compute the extra series yourself or post-process the generated OOXML — do not fall back to a rendered image. Only chart types PowerPoint has no native form for (Sankey, network, chord) go in as images.
- **Default charts render bare** — no title, no data labels, dated palette. Set `showTitle` + `title`, `showValue: true` + `dataLabelPosition`, `chartColors: [...]` from your palette, and quiet the frame (`catAxisLabelColor`/`valAxisLabelColor`, `valGridLine: { color, size }`, `catGridLine: { style: "none" }`, `showLegend: false` for a single series).
- **On a stacked bar or column chart, `dataLabelPosition` must be `ctr`, `inEnd`, or `inBase`.** `outEnd` **corrupts the file**.
- **A combo series using `secondaryValAxis`/`secondaryCatAxis` needs both `valAxes` and `catAxes` on the chart options, two entries each.** Without them pptxgenjs writes axis *ids* it never declares, and PowerPoint **discards that chart** and reports the file as corrupt. Supplying only `valAxes` is not enough.
- **After `writeFile()`, run `python scripts/office/validate.py deck.pptx`.** It reports the two chart faults above and the slide-XML defects PowerPoint refuses, and names the fix for each. Fix them in your generator, not by hand-editing the packed XML.
- **Never reorder the children of `<p:presentation>`.** pptxgenjs writes `<p:notesMasterIdLst>` right after `<p:sldIdLst>` and points both masters at one theme part. PowerPoint reads that happily — move the element and the same deck becomes unopenable.
- **Icons:** render `react-icons` to SVG (`ReactDOMServer.renderToStaticMarkup`), rasterize with `sharp` at ≥256px, and insert via `addImage({ data: "image/png;base64," + buf.toString("base64") })` — the `image/png;base64,` prefix is required (`react-icons`, `react`, `react-dom`, and `sharp` are preinstalled — `npm install react-icons react react-dom sharp` only if a require fails).

## Editing existing decks and templates

Pick layouts first: `python scripts/thumbnail.py template.pptx template-thumbs` writes a labeled grid of every slide and prints the file(s) it created — `template-thumbs.jpg`, split into `template-thumbs-N.jpg` past 12 slides. **Always pass that second argument, named after the deck.** It defaults to `thumbnails`, so two decks thumbnailed in one directory silently overwrite each other's grids — the first deck's are simply gone (template analysis only — visual QA needs the full-resolution renders from [Converting to Images](#converting-to-images); it only accepts `.pptx`, so copy a `.potx` to a `.pptx` name first). Use it with `markitdown` to map each content section onto a template slide, and vary the layouts — don't put every section on the same title-and-bullets slide.

```bash
python3 -c "import sys,zipfile; zipfile.ZipFile(sys.argv[1]).extractall('unpacked')" deck.pptx
python scripts/add_slide.py unpacked/ slide2.xml --after slide2.xml   # duplicate a slide (or slideLayoutN.xml); prints the new slide's path
# reorder / delete slides = edit <p:sldIdLst> in ppt/presentation.xml
python scripts/clean.py unpacked/                                     # after deletions: removes orphaned slides, media, rels
# edit slide content in ppt/slides/slideN.xml
(cd unpacked && rm -f ../out.pptx && zip -Xr ../out.pptx .)           # zip from INSIDE the dir; rm first or deleted parts survive
python scripts/office/validate.py out.pptx --original deck.pptx
```

- **Do all structural work — add, delete, reorder — before editing any slide's content.** `add_slide.py` copies a slide file verbatim, so duplicating after you edit clones the edited content; and `clean.py` deletes any slide missing from `<p:sldIdLst>`, including one you just wrote.
- **Never copy a slide file by hand** — `add_slide.py` does every registration a new slide needs and reports what it made (`Created ppt/slides/slide17.xml from slide2.xml`). It also works directly on a file: `add_slide.py deck.pptx slide2.xml -o out.pptx` — **pass `-o`, or it rewrites the input deck in place.** A duplicated slide still *references* its source's chart/SmartArt/embedded-object parts rather than cloning them, so editing one slide's chart changes the other's.
- **If you use `python-pptx`**, three things it won't do: duplicate a slide (its only entry point is `add_slide(layout)`), preserve formatting through `text_frame.text = "..."` (that collapses the paragraph to a single unstyled run — assign `run.text` instead), or read the SVG/EMF most template art uses (`add_picture` raises `UnidentifiedImageError`).
- Legacy `.ppt` must be converted first: `python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pptx file.ppt`. `.potx` templates unpack and pack identically — keep the `.potx` extension on the output.
- To reuse a template icon or image, duplicate a slide or layout that already contains it.

When filling in a template:

- If you script an XML transform, parse with `defusedxml.minidom` — round-tripping OOXML through `xml.etree.ElementTree` rewrites namespace prefixes and corrupts the deck.
- **Template slots ≠ source items.** If the template shows 4 team members and you have 3, delete the 4th member's entire group (image + text boxes), not just its text — then check for orphaned visuals in QA.
- One `<a:p>` per list item — never concatenate items into a single paragraph. Copy the sibling `<a:pPr>` to preserve spacing, and put `b="1"` on the `<a:rPr>` of titles, section headers, and inline labels (`Status:`, `Owner:`).
- Let bullets inherit from the layout; only add `<a:buChar>`, `<a:buAutoNum>` (numbered), or `<a:buNone>` to override — never a literal `•` in the text.
- Text with leading or trailing spaces needs `xml:space="preserve"` on its `<a:t>`.

## Design Ideas

**Don't create boring slides.** Plain bullets on a white background won't impress anyone. Consider ideas from this list for each slide.

### Before Starting

- **Pick a bold, content-informed color palette**: The palette should feel designed for THIS topic. If swapping your colors into a completely different presentation would still "work," you haven't made specific enough choices.
- **Dominance over equality**: One color should dominate (60-70% visual weight), with 1-2 supporting tones and one sharp accent. Never give all colors equal weight.
- **Dark/light contrast**: Dark backgrounds for title + conclusion slides, light for content ("sandwich" structure). Or commit to dark throughout for a premium feel.
- **Commit to a visual motif**: Pick ONE distinctive element and repeat it — rounded image frames, icons in colored circles. Carry it across every slide. **Do not use a color bar or accent stripe as your motif** (see Avoid list).

### Color Palettes

Choose colors that match your topic — don't default to generic blue. Use these palettes as inspiration:

| Theme | Primary | Secondary | Accent |
|-------|---------|-----------|--------|
| **Midnight Executive** | `1E2761` (navy) | `CADCFC` (ice blue) | `FFFFFF` (white) |
| **Forest & Moss** | `2C5F2D` (forest) | `97BC62` (moss) | `F5F5F5` (cream) |
| **Coral Energy** | `F96167` (coral) | `F9E795` (gold) | `2F3C7E` (navy) |
| **Warm Terracotta** | `B85042` (terracotta) | `E7E8D1` (sand) | `A7BEAE` (sage) |
| **Ocean Gradient** | `065A82` (deep blue) | `1C7293` (teal) | `21295C` (midnight) |
| **Charcoal Minimal** | `36454F` (charcoal) | `F2F2F2` (off-white) | `212121` (black) |
| **Teal Trust** | `028090` (teal) | `00A896` (seafoam) | `02C39A` (mint) |
| **Berry & Cream** | `6D2E46` (berry) | `A26769` (dusty rose) | `ECE2D0` (cream) |
| **Sage Calm** | `84B59F` (sage) | `69A297` (eucalyptus) | `50808E` (slate) |
| **Cherry Bold** | `990011` (cherry) | `FCF6F5` (off-white) | `2F3C7E` (navy) |

### For Each Slide

**Every slide needs a visual element** — image, chart, icon, or shape. Text-only slides are forgettable.

**Layout options:**
- Two-column (text left, illustration on right)
- Icon + text rows (icon in colored circle, bold header, description below)
- 2x2 or 2x3 grid (image on one side, grid of content blocks on other)
- Half-bleed image (full left or right side) with content overlay

**Data display:**
- Large stat callouts (big numbers 60-72pt with small labels below)
- Comparison columns (before/after, pros/cons, side-by-side options)
- Timeline or process flow (numbered steps, arrows)

**Visual polish:**
- Icons in small colored circles next to section headers
- Italic accent text for key stats or taglines

### Typography

**Font names you write into the .pptx are rendered by the user's PowerPoint, not by this environment.** Your visual QA renders via LibreOffice, which substitutes fonts it doesn't have — and for some fonts the substitute has different widths, so your QA preview can show text overflow (or fit) that the real deck won't have. To keep your QA trustworthy:

- **Safe fonts** (render true-to-width in QA *and* ship with Office): **Arial, Calibri, Cambria, Times New Roman, Courier New, Bookman Old Style, Century Schoolbook**. Use these for body text and anything where fit matters.
- **Headers with personality at zero QA risk**: pair a safe-list serif header (Cambria, Bookman Old Style, Century Schoolbook) with a safe-list sans body (Calibri or Arial). You get visual contrast without giving up reliable overflow checks.
- **If the user asks for a font outside the safe list** (e.g. Georgia or Trebuchet MS): use it where the user asked, but size those containers with extra slack (~10%) and don't trust QA text-fit on those elements — the preview of that font is approximate. If the user hasn't specified, prefer safe-list fonts for body text.
- **QA-unreliable fonts** (substitute has different widths — overflow checks can be wrong): Georgia, Trebuchet MS, Impact, Arial Black, Garamond, Consolas, Palatino Linotype. Calibri Light substitution varies by environment; treat as QA-unreliable. Fine for titles/accents with slack; don't trust QA text-fit on these.
- **Never default to Aptos** — Office's post-2023 default has no metric-compatible substitute here *and* is missing from older Office installs, so it's unreliable on both ends.

| Element | Size |
|---------|------|
| Slide title | 36-44pt bold |
| Section header | 20-24pt bold |
| Body text | 14-16pt |
| Captions | 10-12pt muted |

### Spacing

- 0.5" minimum margins
- 0.3-0.5" between content blocks
- Leave breathing room—don't fill every inch

### Avoid (Common Mistakes)

- **Don't repeat the same layout** — vary columns, cards, and callouts across slides
- **Don't center body text** — left-align paragraphs and lists; center only titles
- **Don't skimp on size contrast** — titles need 36pt+ to stand out from 14-16pt body
- **Don't default to blue** — pick colors that reflect the specific topic
- **Don't mix spacing randomly** — choose 0.3" or 0.5" gaps and use consistently
- **Don't style one slide and leave the rest plain** — commit fully or keep it simple throughout
- **Don't create text-only slides** — add images, icons, charts, or visual elements; avoid plain title + bullets
- **Don't forget text box padding** — when aligning lines or shapes with text edges, set `margin: 0` on the text box or offset the shape to account for padding
- **Don't use low-contrast elements** — icons AND text need strong contrast against the background; avoid light text on light backgrounds or dark text on dark backgrounds
- **NEVER use accent lines under titles** — these are a hallmark of AI-generated slides; use whitespace or background color instead
- **NEVER add decorative color bars or accent stripes** — this includes: header/footer bars spanning the slide width, vertical sidebar stripes down one edge of the slide, thin accent stripes along one edge of a card or content block, and "single-side borders" on rectangles. These read as AI-generated filler. If you want to set a card apart, use a subtle background tint, a drop shadow, or an icon — not an edge stripe.
- **Don't default to cream/beige backgrounds** — when no background is specified, use white (`FFFFFF`) or the user's brand palette; avoid warm-neutral defaults like `F5F5DC`, `FAF0E6`, `FAEBD7`, `FFF8E1`
- **Don't ship text that overflows its shape** — if text doesn't fit, reduce font size, split across slides, or enlarge the container; never leave content cut off or spilling past bounds

## QA (Required)

Your first render usually has a few real issues — overlaps, overflow, misalignment. Find and fix those, re-render only the slides you changed, and stop.

### Content QA

```bash
markitdown output.pptx
```

Check for missing content, typos, wrong order.

**When using templates, check for leftover placeholder text:**

```bash
markitdown output.pptx | grep -iE "\bx{3,}\b|lorem|ipsum|\bTODO|\[insert|this.*(page|slide).*layout"
```

If grep returns results, fix them before declaring success.

### File QA (required)

```bash
python scripts/office/validate.py output.pptx                      # built from scratch
python scripts/office/validate.py output.pptx --original src.pptx  # built from a template
```

**If the deck came from a template, always pass `--original`.** A template may itself
contain parts the XSD rejects, so a bare run can report failures you never caused — and
a genuine regression can hide among them. `--original` baselines
the schema and slide checks against the template, suppressing errors it already had.
The structural checks — relationships, content types, charts — ignore `--original` and
report template-inherited problems either way, so read those on their own merits.

pptxgenjs emits chart XML PowerPoint refuses to open, and every other tool
accepts: python-pptx opens those decks, LibreOffice renders them, the XSD
passes them. Every failure names its fix. Fix it in the generator and rebuild.

### Visual QA

Convert the slides to images (see [Converting to Images](#converting-to-images)) and inspect every one. After staring at the generating code you tend to see what you expect rather than what rendered, so look at the images fresh (a subagent works well for this if you have one). User-visible defects to look for:

- **Text overflow or text cut off at a box or slide boundary — check this first.** It is the most common defect and always user-visible. (For a font the previewer renders unreliably per Typography, the preview is approximate: trust the ~10% slack you left, not its apparent fit.)
- Overlapping elements (text through shapes, lines through words, stacked elements)
- Source citations or footers colliding with content above
- Elements too close (< 0.3" gaps) or cards/sections nearly touching
- Uneven gaps (large empty area in one place, cramped in another)
- Insufficient margin from slide edges (< 0.5")
- Columns or similar elements not aligned consistently
- Low-contrast text (e.g., light gray text on cream-colored background)
- Template decoration mispositioned after text replacement — e.g., a title underline positioned for one line, but the replaced title wrapped to two
- Low-contrast icons (e.g., dark icons on dark backgrounds without a contrasting circle)
- Text boxes too narrow causing excessive wrapping
- Leftover placeholder content

Convert presentations to individual slide images for visual inspection:

```bash
python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf output.pptx

   Delivered as a full app: FastAPI backend streaming live progress to a Vue.js frontend.

I've gone through the whole folder and both prior chat sessions. Here's where things stand.

## The project

**A Multi-Agent Agentic RAG Platform for Automated Literature Review** ("ResearchGPT") — GRIET, Dept. of Data Science, batch DSC06. You (P. Sreekaran Reddy), Abrarullah Mohammed, G. Shashivadan Rao. Guide: Dr. S. Govinda Rao. Target submission ~2026-09-05.

Six agents in a LangGraph state machine — Planner → Retriever → Ingest → Rank → Extractor → Verifier → Critic → HITL → Writer, with a bounded 3-iteration critic loop. Vue 3 SPA + FastAPI (REST + SSE).

**Five hard constraints** that drive everything: zero API budget, CPU-only machine, a model-training component is required, grading weights *working + not hallucinating* over paper polish, and Vue.js frontend is mandatory.

## What exists on disk

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `SESSION_CONTEXT.md` | The canonical handoff — read-this-first record of the 2026-08-06 session |
| `RESEARCHGPT_SPEC.md` | Original master spec (pre-dates the constraints; has known errors) |
| `PROJECT_PLAN.md` | 30-day execution plan, descope ladder, evaluation design |
| `LITERATURE_REVIEW.md` | 25 papers 2023–2026, comparative table, 3 ranked base-paper candidates |
| `PAPER_ANALYSIS.md` (90 KB) | Per-paper 6-field analysis |
| `PAPER_DEEP_DIVE.md` (140 KB) | Full-text dive — 18 of 26 papers in full text, every reported number, verbatim limitations |
| `ARCHITECTURE_REVIEW.md` | Audit of the diagrams + corrected UML, PPT consistency table |
| `diagrams/*.drawio` (2) | UML activity diagram (33 vertices) and UML component diagram (27 vertices) |
| `Literature papers/` | 7 PDFs |
| `Review-1 dsc06.pptx` | 16 slides, completed review |
| **`Template - PWP1 - Review 2.pptx`** | **New — added today, 20-slide blank template** |

**Status: zero code written.** Implementation is still at Day 0, and the 30-day clock started 2026-08-06 — you're 3 days in.

## The new thing: Review-2 template

That template landed today and it's a much heavier ask than Review-1:

- Literature survey **table** — 20–25 approaches with Problem / Dataset / Algorithm / Metrics / Advantages / Limitations
- **Plus** a description slide per approach in "22322" format (2 sentences intro, 2 objective, 3 methodology, 2 results, 2 limitations) — that's ~20 extra slides
- Limitations summary: 8–10 points, categorised (dataset / algorithm / deployment issues)
- Research gap (4–7 points, incl. an Existing-Findings → Limitations → Gap table)
- Problem statement, refined objectives, software/hardware
- Architecture diagram + explanation slides; MCD + explanation slides
- IEEE-style references

Good news: `LITERATURE_REVIEW.md` + `PAPER_ANALYSIS.md` + `PAPER_DEEP_DIVE.md` already contain essentially all the raw material for the survey slides, and both diagrams are already drawn.

## Three things carried over that still need your decision

1. **Base paper switch (Aytar → SurveyGen).** The current base paper is mis-described in the spec — its real title is *"A synergistic multi-stage RAG architecture…"*; it optimises retrieval precision, it doesn't generate reviews. The extension narrative's "fixed single-pass pipeline" claim is factually wrong about it. Needs your guide's sign-off.
2. **MCD notation** — classical structure chart (what your slide 12 describes) or UML component diagram (what the rubric's "standard notation" implies). Both are prepared; slide 12's ○/● explanation only works for the structure chart.
3. **Human-in-the-loop stays in Objective 2 only if you build it** (~half a day: dropped-claims confirm/override panel).

## Two visible errors in Review-1 that must not survive into Review-2

- Slide 6: **"GPU: 8GB Minimum"** — your machine is CPU-only. You've specified hardware you don't have.
- Slide 8: **"Extractor chunks and embeds them"** — that's the Ingestor's job. As written, the system has no structured extraction at all, which deletes a main contribution.

Also: pgvector/PostgreSQL on slides 3, 8, 9 vs Chroma everywhere else, and Semantic Scholar as a source (confirmed HTTP 429 without a key).

Two workstreams are now competing for the same days: **building the Review-2 deck** and **starting the code** (Day 1 in the plan is scaffolding + `core/llm.py` with cache/throttle/backoff, register two free LLM tiers, download SciFact). The Day-12 milestone — a complete cited review from the CLI — is the insurance policy and shouldn't slip.

102	| 22 | Min et al. 2023 (FActScore) | EMNLP `C` | Binary factuality judgements are inadequate for long text | Decompose generation into **atomic facts**; % supported by a knowledge source | **The method your Verifier implements.** Automated estimator <2% error | Needs a reliable knowledge source; biography domain | People biographies; 13 LMs, 6,500 generations | [10.18653/v1/2023.emnlp-main.741](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2023.emnlp-main.741) |
103	| 23 | Gao et al. 2023 (ALCE) | EMNLP `C` | No reproducible benchmark for citation quality | ALCE benchmark; automatic metrics for fluency / correctness / citation quality | Correlates with human judgement; gives you a citation-accuracy metric | **Best models lack full citation support 50% of the time** — sobering | ELI5 (named); ALCE benchmark | [10.18653/v1/2023.emnlp-main.398](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2023.emnlp-main.398) |
104	| 24 | Huang et al. 2024 | ACM TOIS `J` | Hallucination literature lacks a unified taxonomy | Survey: taxonomy, causes, detection methods, benchmarks, mitigation | 1,700+ citations; explicitly covers RAG's *limits* in fighting hallucination | Survey; no new method | None | [10.1145/3703155](https://doi.org/10.1145/3703155) |
105	| 25 | Liu et al. 2024 (CliVER) | JAMIA Open `J` | Scientific claim verification is manual | Retrieve abstracts → extract sentences → PICO framing → 3-model ensemble (support/refute/neutral) | F1 0.92 on own set; **benchmarked against 4 clinicians** | Drops to 63.2% label accuracy vs clinicians on real claims | CoVERt (own), SciFact, 189,648 PubMed abstracts | [10.1093/jamiaopen/ooae021](https://doi.org/10.1093/jamiaopen/ooae021) |
106	
107	---
108	
109	## 4. Thematic synthesis
110	
111	### C1 — RAG foundations (papers 1–4)
112	Huang & Huang's four-stage taxonomy (pre-retrieval / retrieval / post-retrieval / generation) is the cleanest scaffold for describing your pipeline, and using a *Computing Surveys* taxonomy rather than inventing your own strengthens the design chapter. Peng et al. matter mainly as a **negative justification**: GraphRAG is the current frontier in structural retrieval, and citing it lets you explain why a flat hybrid index is adequate at your corpus size instead of looking unaware. Lyu et al. is the argument that evaluating only the generator is insufficient — support for your component-wise ablations. Siriwardhana et al. shows joint retriever–generator training is the strongest domain-adaptation route and that **you are explicitly not taking it** ($0, CPU-only); cite it when defending frozen retrieval.
113	
114	### C2 — Agentic and self-reflective RAG (papers 5–9)
115	This cluster establishes that adaptive control beats fixed pipelines. **Adaptive-RAG** is the strongest precedent for your Planner: a small classifier routing between no-retrieval, single-step and iterative strategies. **Ammann et al. is your single closest methodological relative** — LLM query decomposition, per-sub-question retrieval, cross-encoder reranking of a merged pool, explicitly *"without any extra training or specialized indexing."* That is your Planner + Retriever, and their +36.7% MRR@10 / +11.6% F1 gives you a published expectation to compare against. Treat it as a baseline, not just a citation. **Chain-of-Note** contributes the refusal behaviour your §9.5 stress test demonstrates: a system that answers "unknown" rather than inventing. Li et al. (IP&M) appears methodologically close, but **its abstract could not be retrieved and its claims are unverified** — read it before relying on it.
116	
117	### C3 — Multi-agent LLM systems (papers 10–12)
118	Thinner than the other clusters, and honestly so: rigorous peer-reviewed multi-agent work is concentrated in software engineering and robotics, not document synthesis. ChatDev is the canonical demonstration that role specialisation plus structured communication outperforms monolithic prompting. Li et al.'s five-component framework gives you standard vocabulary. AutoHMA-LLM is the most useful of the three for your report because it publishes the *efficiency* numbers multi-agent systems are usually criticised for hiding (−46% communication steps, −31% token usage) — exactly the objection a reviewer will raise about six agents. **The absence of peer-reviewed multi-agent work on literature review is itself a gap you should claim (§5).**
119	
120	### C4 — Scientific document understanding (papers 13–15)
121	Dagdelen et al. in *Nature Communications* is the strongest possible precedent for structured JSON extraction from scientific text, and it validates your four-field schema as an established design rather than an invention. **Sarol et al. is the most important paper in this document for calibrating your expectations**: it is essentially your Verifier, built carefully with BM25 + MonoT5 + fine-tuned MultiVerS, and it reaches only **0.59 micro-F1**. If your fine-tuned verifier reports 0.9+ on real citations, something is wrong with your evaluation. Li et al. proves empirically that conditioning on abstracts rather than full-text spans *teaches models to hallucinate* — a direct argument for your `evidence_spans` design and against the abstract-only degraded mode in `PROJECT_PLAN.md`.
122	
123	### C5 — Automated survey generation (papers 16–20)
124	The cluster your work sits in. SciReviewGen supplies the dataset; SurveyGen supplies both a newer dataset and the quality-aware retrieval baseline; CiteBench supplies evaluation discipline. Bolaños et al. is strategically valuable because it maps 21 existing SLR tools — use it to position ResearchGPT against real systems rather than against a strawman. Valsci is the most direct competitor: open-source, self-hostable, SciFact-evaluated, explicitly targeting citation hallucination. **You must cite and compare against Valsci or a reviewer will ask why you didn't.**
125	
126	### C6 — Grounding and verification (papers 21–25)
127	This cluster underwrites your graded criterion. FActScore is the method your Verifier implements — atomic decomposition plus per-fact support checking — and citing it means your design is a recognised technique, not an ad-hoc filter. ALCE supplies the citation-quality metrics and the sobering finding that top systems fail full citation support half the time. Huang et al.'s survey covers the limits of RAG as a hallucination remedy, which you need for an honest limitations section. CliVER is the most useful methodologically: a three-way ensemble reaching F1 0.92 on its own data but only **63.2% against clinicians on real claims** — the clearest available evidence that in-domain benchmark scores overstate real-world verification accuracy.
128	
129	---
130	
131	## 5. Research gaps
132	
133	Ordered by how directly ResearchGPT addresses them. Gaps 1–3 are defensible contribution claims; 4–5 are honest openings you may not fill this cycle.
134	
135	**Gap 1 — No peer-reviewed multi-agent architecture for literature review generation.**
136	C3 demonstrates role specialisation in software engineering (ChatDev) and robotics (AutoHMA-LLM). C5 shows review generation is done with single-pass RAG pipelines (SurveyGen's QUAL-SG, Valsci's guided prompt-flow). **The intersection is empty in the peer-reviewed 2023–2026 literature.** This is your primary claim, and this review is the evidence for it.
137	
138	**Gap 2 — Verification is a separate literature from review generation.**
139	C6 develops claim-level grounding (FActScore, ALCE) and C4 applies it to citations (Sarol et al.), but no C5 system embeds atomic-claim verification as a *control mechanism* that removes unsupported content before writing. Valsci verifies claims but doesn't synthesise; SurveyGen synthesises but reports low citation quality. ResearchGPT's Verifier-as-filter sits exactly in that gap.
140	
141	**Gap 3 — No bounded feedback loop with explicit stop criteria.**
142	Adaptive-RAG routes *once*, per query. Self-BioRAG self-reflects *within* a generation. Neither implements an iteration-capped outer loop that can send control back to planning based on a coverage assessment. Your Critic with `max_iterations=3` and forced-WRITE termination is genuinely unoccupied territory.
143	
144	**Gap 4 — Structured per-paper extraction is not applied to review generation.**
145	Dagdelen et al. show LLMs can produce structured JSON records from scientific text; C5 systems still emit free text. Your four-field schema bridges these, though the contribution is smaller than 1–3 since it is an application of an established technique.
146	
147	**Gap 5 — Evaluation of generated reviews is unsettled and partly circular.**
148	RAGAs is reference-free but LLM-judged; ALCE needs annotated corpora; SurveyGen relies on human evaluation. Nobody has a trusted automatic measure of review quality. This gap constrains *you* as much as it opens an opportunity — it is why `PROJECT_PLAN.md §9.6` insists your groundedness number be measured independently rather than by your own Verifier.
149	
150	**Two absences worth naming honestly in your Limitations section:**
151	- **Cost- and hardware-constrained agentic RAG is essentially unstudied.** Every system above assumes frontier-model API access. Your $0, CPU-only constraint is unusual — which makes it a modest novelty, but also means there is no baseline to compare against.
152	- **Domain shift in scientific claim verification is under-reported.** SciFact and CliVER are biomedical; your corpus is CS. CliVER's 0.92→63.2% drop is the warning sign, and no paper in this set measures cross-domain verifier transfer.
153	
154	---
155	
156	## 6. Verification report
157	
158	**Method.** Each DOI was resolved through the OpenAlex works API; the base paper was additionally confirmed via Crossref author+container query. Abstracts came from OpenAlex `abstract_inverted_index`, Semantic Scholar, or the ACL Anthology record. Search used OpenAlex `title_and_abstract.search` with a hard `2023-01-01 … 2026-12-31` publication-date filter, across 6 thematic clusters and 28 named-system queries (~712 unique works screened).
159	
160	**Results.** 35 DOIs fetched, **0 resolution failures**. All 25 main-table papers resolved to a peer-reviewed journal or Scopus-indexed proceedings. **All are within the 2023–2026 window.**
161	
162	**⚠️ Flagged — verified record, unverified content (1 paper):**
163	
164	| Paper | Issue |
165	|---|---|
166	| #8 Li et al. 2025, *Inf. Process. Manag.*, [10.1016/j.ipm.2025.104369](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ipm.2025.104369) | DOI, title, authors, venue and year confirmed in OpenAlex **and** Semantic Scholar. **Abstract absent from both.** Its Problem/Methodology/Dataset cells derive from the title only. **Read the paper before citing it.** Note: Semantic Scholar dates it 2026, OpenAlex 2025 — confirm the year before it enters your reference list. |
167	
168	**Excluded — preprint-only (not in main table).** The sweep found ~70 arXiv-only works, including several the field treats as canonical — Self-RAG, Corrective RAG, RAPTOR, AutoSurvey, MetaGPT, the Gao et al. RAG survey. Per your constraint these are omitted from the main table. Two consequences worth weighing:
169	
170	- Self-RAG and Corrective RAG are the most-cited self-reflective RAG systems in existence. A reviewer may expect them. If you cite them, label `[preprint]` as your constraint requires and keep them out of the comparative table.
171	- Your spec §1.5 notes Self-RAG was resolved "via OpenReview." **ICLR/NeurIPS OpenReview papers are peer-reviewed and Scopus-indexed** — if Self-RAG's ICLR 2024 version is what you cite, it is *not* a preprint and belongs in the main table. Worth confirming; I could not establish a non-arXiv DOI for it via OpenAlex.
172	
173	**Verified reserve pool (9 papers).** Fully resolved, in-window, peer-reviewed, but cut for balance. Use as substitutes:
174	
175	| Paper | Venue | DOI |
176	|---|---|---|
177	| Zhang et al. 2025, LongCite (sentence-level citations) | ACL Findings | [10.18653/v1/2025.findings-acl.264](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.findings-acl.264) |
178	| Yan et al. 2025, Atomic Fact Decomposition for Attributed QA | IEEE TKDE | [10.1109/tkde.2025.3608716](https://doi.org/10.1109/tkde.2025.3608716) |

181	| Ofori-Boateng et al. 2024, SR automation review | Artif. Intell. Rev. | [10.1007/s10462-024-10844-w](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10462-024-10844-w) |
182	| Khraisha et al. 2024, Can LLMs replace humans in SRs? | Research Synthesis Methods | [10.1002/jrsm.1715](https://doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.1715) |
183	| Luo et al. 2023, CitationSum | ACM (WWW) | [10.1145/3543507.3583505](https://doi.org/10.1145/3543507.3583505) |

189	## 7. Three things to act on
190	
191	1. **Fix `RESEARCHGPT_SPEC.md §1.2 and §1.3.** The base paper is a multi-stage data-science RAG architecture, not literature assistance, and the "fixed single-pass pipeline" row is wrong.

Against real citations that would be an outlier, not a success — so measure it independently, or you will be defending a number that looks too good.
