# Literature Review — Multi-Agent Agentic RAG for Automated Literature Review

> **Scope.** 25 papers, published 2023–2026, on agentic/multi-agent RAG, scientific document synthesis, automated review generation, and claim-level grounding. Plus 3 ranked candidate base papers (2024–2026 only).
>
> **Verification.** Every entry below was resolved against the **OpenAlex** and **Crossref** APIs by DOI; abstracts were pulled from OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, or the ACL Anthology record. No citation in this document was written from memory. Where an abstract did not state something (e.g. dataset names), the field says so rather than guessing.
>
> **Venue policy.** In computer science the leading venues are conferences, not journals — ACL, NAACL, EMNLP, EACL and AAAI proceedings are Scopus-indexed and are treated here as peer-reviewed. Every paper in the main table appeared in a peer-reviewed journal or Scopus-indexed proceedings. **There are no arXiv-only preprints in the main table** (see §6).
>
> *Compiled 2026-08-06. Companion to `RESEARCHGPT_SPEC.md` and `PROJECT_PLAN.md`.*

---

## 1. ⚠️ Finding that affects your spec: the base paper is not what §1.2 says it is

`RESEARCHGPT_SPEC.md §1.2` describes the base paper as *"Aytar et al. (2025), Natural Language Processing Journal — RAG-based literature assistance."*

The paper is real and correctly attributed, but its actual content differs:

> **Aytar, A. Y., Kaya, K., & Kılıç, K. (2025).** "A synergistic multi-stage RAG architecture for boosting context relevance in data science literature." *Natural Language Processing Journal*, Elsevier. DOI: [10.1016/j.nlp.2025.100179](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nlp.2025.100179)

From the verified abstract, the system integrates **GROBID structured parsing, domain-specific embedding fine-tuning from textbooks, semantic chunking, and an "Abstract First" retrieval strategy**, evaluated with **RAGAS** on a custom data-science query set, reporting a **>15-fold improvement in Context Relevance** over baseline RAG.

Two consequences you must act on:

1. **Your extension table (§1.3) contains a factual error.** It claims the base paper's retrieval control is a *"fixed single-pass pipeline."* It is explicitly a **multi-stage** architecture. A reviewer who reads the base paper will catch this immediately, and it is the row your whole "we are more agentic" narrative rests on. Rewrite that row.
2. **The task doesn't match.** Aytar et al. improve *context relevance for retrieval in the data-science domain*. They do not generate literature reviews. Positioning ResearchGPT as an extension means arguing across a task boundary, which is harder than it needs to be — see §2 for two better-fitting candidates.

Note also that Aytar et al. use **GROBID**, which `PROJECT_PLAN.md §2.2` cuts. If you keep Aytar as the base paper, dropping GROBID becomes a deviation you must defend rather than a free simplification.

---

## 2. Base paper candidates (2024–2026), ranked

### 🥇 Rank 1 — SurveyGen / QUAL-SG

**Bao, T., Nayeem, M. T., Rafiei, D., & Zhang, C. (2025).** "SurveyGen: Quality-Aware Scientific Survey Generation with Large Language Models." *Proceedings of EMNLP 2025 (Main)*. DOI: [10.18653/v1/2025.emnlp-main.136](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.emnlp-main.136)
**Venue:** EMNLP main conference · ACL Anthology · Scopus-indexed proceedings · verified via OpenAlex + ACL Anthology

**Why it is the cleanest extension target.** Same task as yours — automatic scientific survey generation. They build QUAL-SG, which *"enhances the standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline by incorporating quality-aware indicators into literature retrieval to assess and select higher-quality source papers"* — which is precisely your venue-tier ranking (spec §11), meaning you have a directly comparable component rather than an analogy.

Decisively, **their own stated conclusion is your problem statement**: *"fully automatic survey generation still suffers from low citation quality and limited critical analysis."* Your Verifier attacks low citation quality; your Critic and four-field extraction schema attack limited critical analysis. You are not asserting a gap — you are citing the base paper's authors asserting it. That is the strongest possible extension narrative.

They also release **4,200+ human-written surveys and 242,143 cited references**, giving you an evaluation resource with the same provenance as your base paper.

*Extension claim:* QUAL-SG is a single-pass quality-aware RAG pipeline. ResearchGPT adds (a) agentic replanning, (b) claim-level verification with unsupported-claim removal, (c) a bounded critic loop, (d) structured per-paper extraction — each targeting a deficiency they report.

### 🥈 Rank 2 — Valsci

**Edelman, B., & Skolnick, J. (2025).** "Valsci: an open-source, self-hostable literature review utility for automated large-batch scientific claim verification using large language models." *BMC Bioinformatics*, 26. DOI: [10.1186/s12859-025-06159-4](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12859-025-06159-4)
**Venue:** BMC Bioinformatics · Springer Nature · Scopus-indexed journal (Q1/Q2) · verified via OpenAlex

**Why it fits.** It unites *"retrieval-augmented generation with structured bibliometric scoring and chain-of-thought prompting"* for literature-based claim verification, evaluated on **SciFact** — the exact dataset `PROJECT_PLAN.md §4.2` uses to train your verifier. It reports outperforming base GPT-4o *"in citation hallucination rate while maintaining a low misclassification rate,"* giving you a published anti-hallucination baseline to beat on shared data.

*Extension claim:* Valsci verifies claims but does not synthesise a review; it is a single guided prompt-flow, not a multi-agent graph, and its verifier is a prompted LLM rather than a trained model. ResearchGPT adds review synthesis, agentic control, and a fine-tuned local verifier.

*Weakness as base paper:* biomedical framing, and the output is a verification report rather than a literature review.

### 🥉 Rank 3 — Aytar et al. (your spec's current choice)

**Aytar, A. Y., Kaya, K., & Kılıç, K. (2025).** *Natural Language Processing Journal.* DOI: [10.1016/j.nlp.2025.100179](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nlp.2025.100179)
**Venue:** Elsevier · Scopus-indexed journal · verified via Crossref + OpenAlex

Retained because it is Scopus-indexed, Elsevier-published, recent, and already embedded in your spec. But it ranks third: the task is context-relevance optimisation, not review generation; it is already multi-stage, which blunts the "we are more agentic" claim; and at the time of checking it had very few citations, so it carries less weight as a foundation than an EMNLP main-conference paper.

**Recommendation:** switch the base paper to **SurveyGen (Rank 1)** and demote Aytar et al. to a closely-related work you compare against. If your supervisor has already approved Aytar, keep it but **fix the §1.3 table row** and add SurveyGen as the primary comparison point.

---

## 3. Comparative table — 25 papers

`J` = journal · `C` = Scopus-indexed conference proceedings. Cells are compressed; full annotations in §4.

Surv. `J` | RAG research fragmented across sub-stages | Survey; 4-stage taxonomy: pre-retrieval / retrieval / post-retrieval / generation | Gives the stage vocabulary your architecture chapter needs | Survey — no new system or results | None | [10.1145/3805774](https://doi.org/10.1145/3805774) |

## 4. Thematic synthesis

### C1 — RAG foundations (papers 1–4)
Huang & Huang's four-stage taxonomy (pre-retrieval / retrieval / post-retrieval / generation) is the cleanest scaffold for describing your pipeline, and using a *Computing Surveys* taxonomy rather than inventing your own strengthens the design chapter. Peng et al. matter mainly as a **negative justification**: GraphRAG is the current frontier in structural retrieval, and citing it lets you explain why a flat hybrid index is adequate at your corpus size instead of looking unaware. Lyu et al. is the argument that evaluating only the generator is insufficient — support for your component-wise ablations. Siriwardhana et al. shows joint retriever–generator training is the strongest domain-adaptation route and that **you are explicitly not taking it** ($0, CPU-only); cite it when defending frozen retrieval.

### C2 — Agentic and self-reflective RAG (papers 5–9)
This cluster establishes that adaptive control beats fixed pipelines. **Adaptive-RAG** is the strongest precedent for your Planner: a small classifier routing between no-retrieval, single-step and iterative strategies. **Ammann et al. is your single closest methodological relative** — LLM query decomposition, per-sub-question retrieval, cross-encoder reranking of a merged pool, explicitly *"without any extra training or specialized indexing."* That is your Planner + Retriever, and their +36.7% MRR@10 / +11.6% F1 gives you a published expectation to compare against. Treat it as a baseline, not just a citation. **Chain-of-Note** contributes the refusal behaviour your §9.5 stress test demonstrates: a system that answers "unknown" rather than inventing. Li et al. (IP&M) appears methodologically close, but **its abstract could not be retrieved and its claims are unverified** — read it before relying on it.

### C3 — Multi-agent LLM systems (papers 10–12)
Thinner than the other clusters, and honestly so: rigorous peer-reviewed multi-agent work is concentrated in software engineering and robotics, not document synthesis. ChatDev is the canonical demonstration that role specialisation plus structured communication outperforms monolithic prompting. Li et al.'s five-component framework gives you standard vocabulary. AutoHMA-LLM is the most useful of the three for your report because it publishes the *efficiency* numbers multi-agent systems are usually criticised for hiding (−46% communication steps, −31% token usage) — exactly the objection a reviewer will raise about six agents. **The absence of peer-reviewed multi-agent work on literature review is itself a gap you should claim (§5).**

### C4 — Scientific document understanding (papers 13–15)
Dagdelen et al. in *Nature Communications* is the strongest possible precedent for structured JSON extraction from scientific text, and it validates your four-field schema as an established design rather than an invention. **Sarol et al. is the most important paper in this document for calibrating your expectations**: it is essentially your Verifier, built carefully with BM25 + MonoT5 + fine-tuned MultiVerS, and it reaches only **0.59 micro-F1**. If your fine-tuned verifier reports 0.9+ on real citations, something is wrong with your evaluation. Li et al. proves empirically that conditioning on abstracts rather than full-text spans *teaches models to hallucinate* — a direct argument for your `evidence_spans` design and against the abstract-only degraded mode in `PROJECT_PLAN.md`.

### C5 — Automated survey generation (papers 16–20)
The cluster your work sits in. SciReviewGen supplies the dataset; SurveyGen supplies both a newer dataset and the quality-aware retrieval baseline; CiteBench supplies evaluation discipline. Bolaños et al. is strategically valuable because it maps 21 existing SLR tools — use it to position ResearchGPT against real systems rather than against a strawman. Valsci is the most direct competitor: open-source, self-hostable, SciFact-evaluated, explicitly targeting citation hallucination. **You must cite and compare against Valsci or a reviewer will ask why you didn't.**

### C6 — Grounding and verification (papers 21–25)
This cluster underwrites your graded criterion. FActScore is the method your Verifier implements — atomic decomposition plus per-fact support checking — and citing it means your design is a recognised technique, not an ad-hoc filter. ALCE supplies the citation-quality metrics and the sobering finding that top systems fail full citation support half the time. Huang et al.'s survey covers the limits of RAG as a hallucination remedy, which you need for an honest limitations section. CliVER is the most useful methodologically: a three-way ensemble reaching F1 0.92 on its own data but only **63.2% against clinicians on real claims** — the clearest available evidence that in-domain benchmark scores overstate real-world verification accuracy.

---

## 5. Research gaps

Ordered by how directly ResearchGPT addresses them. Gaps 1–3 are defensible contribution claims; 4–5 are honest openings you may not fill this cycle.

**Gap 1 — No peer-reviewed multi-agent architecture for literature review generation.**
C3 demonstrates role specialisation in software engineering (ChatDev) and robotics (AutoHMA-LLM). C5 shows review generation is done with single-pass RAG pipelines (SurveyGen's QUAL-SG, Valsci's guided prompt-flow). **The intersection is empty in the peer-reviewed 2023–2026 literature.** This is your primary claim, and this review is the evidence for it.

**Gap 2 — Verification is a separate literature from review generation.**
C6 develops claim-level grounding (FActScore, ALCE) and C4 applies it to citations (Sarol et al.), but no C5 system embeds atomic-claim verification as a *control mechanism* that removes unsupported content before writing. Valsci verifies claims but doesn't synthesise; SurveyGen synthesises but reports low citation quality. ResearchGPT's Verifier-as-filter sits exactly in that gap.

**Gap 3 — No bounded feedback loop with explicit stop criteria.**
Adaptive-RAG routes *once*, per query. Self-BioRAG self-reflects *within* a generation. Neither implements an iteration-capped outer loop that can send control back to planning based on a coverage assessment. Your Critic with `max_iterations=3` and forced-WRITE termination is genuinely unoccupied territory.

**Gap 4 — Structured per-paper extraction is not applied to review generation.**
Dagdelen et al. show LLMs can produce structured JSON records from scientific text; C5 systems still emit free text. Your four-field schema bridges these, though the contribution is smaller than 1–3 since it is an application of an established technique.

**Gap 5 — Evaluation of generated reviews is unsettled and partly circular.**
RAGAs is reference-free but LLM-judged; ALCE needs annotated corpora; SurveyGen relies on human evaluation. Nobody has a trusted automatic measure of review quality. This gap constrains *you* as much as it opens an opportunity — it is why `PROJECT_PLAN.md §9.6` insists your groundedness number be measured independently rather than by your own Verifier.

**Two absences worth naming honestly in your Limitations section:**
- **Cost- and hardware-constrained agentic RAG is essentially unstudied.** Every system above assumes frontier-model API access. Your $0, CPU-only constraint is unusual — which makes it a modest novelty, but also means there is no baseline to compare against.
- **Domain shift in scientific claim verification is under-reported.** SciFact and CliVER are biomedical; your corpus is CS. CliVER's 0.92→63.2% drop is the warning sign, and no paper in this set measures cross-domain verifier transfer.

---

2	
3	> **What this is.** An extensive summary of *what is actually inside each paper* — architecture details, experimental setup, every reported number, ablations, and the authors' own verbatim limitations. This goes beyond `PAPER_ANALYSIS.md`, which was written from abstracts.
4	>
5	> **How the papers were obtained.** PDFs downloaded from ACL Anthology, Springer, Nature and BMC; full text for two paywalled biomedical papers retrieved from **Europe PMC** (`PMC11231046`, `PMC10919922`); TACL located on ACL Anthology (`2023.tacl-1.1`). Text extracted with PyMuPDF, reference lists trimmed.
6	>
7	> ### ⚠️ Coverage — read this first
8	>
9	> **18 of 26 papers were obtained in full text.** The remaining **8 are abstract-only** because the publisher blocked automated access (HTTP 403) or the paper is paywalled with no OA route:
10	>
11	> | Abstract-only | Reason |

13	> | **BASE** Aytar et al. | Elsevier, no OA |

28	## The five most important things the full texts revealed
29	
30	These did not appear in any abstract and change decisions in `PROJECT_PLAN.md`.
31	
32	**1. Your closest competitor names your contribution as its own limitation.** Ammann et al. (C2-09) — the paper whose pipeline most resembles your Planner+Retriever — list under Limitations: *"Lack of iterative retrieval. Our pipeline operates in a single-shot manner: subqueries are generated once and not updated based on retrieved evidence. This limits its ability to support adaptive multi-step reasoning."* That is exactly what your Critic loop does. **Quote it verbatim in your Introduction.**
33	
34	**2. Humans barely agree on citation accuracy.** Sarol et al. (C4-14) report inter-annotator agreement of **0.18–0.31** on accuracy labels and **0.20–0.37** on evidence sentences — "fair" at best, between trained annotators on a carefully designed task. This reframes your entire evaluation: if expert humans agree only ~0.3, a verifier scoring 0.59 F1 against them is not obviously worse than a human, and your own 2-annotator Likert study (`PROJECT_PLAN.md §9.5`) should report agreement, not just means.
35	
36	**3. Abstract-only conditioning costs 21 points of faithfulness — measured.** Li et al. (C4-15) report ANLI faithfulness of generated citations: **Abstract 0.745 vs. Context-CTS 0.959, Oracle-CTS 0.940, Keyword-CTS 0.941.** Your abstract-only degraded mode is not a mild compromise; it is the single largest faithfulness regression in this literature.
37	
38	**4. Structured extraction needs ~20 examples to stabilise.** Dagdelen et al. (C4-13) found *"output sequences are not properly structured for training set sizes below ~10 samples, but there is a sharp increase in the number of correctly structured outputs at ~20 samples, which seems to be the minimum number of examples GPT-3 needs to learn a desired output format."* Directly sets the few-shot example count for your Extractor prompt.
39	
40	**5. Adaptive-RAG's classifier is the weak link, by their own admission.** They report a measurable gap between their trained classifier and an oracle classifier, and state *"there is still room to improve the effectiveness of the classifier."* If you build a router, expect it — not the retrieval — to be your bottleneck.

46	## Aytar, Kaya & Kılıç (2025) — Synergistic Multi-Stage RAG **[ABSTRACT ONLY]**
47	
48	**Citation.** Aytar, A. Y., Kaya, K., & Kılıç, K. (2025). "A synergistic multi-stage RAG architecture for boosting context relevance in data science literature." *Natural Language Processing Journal* (Elsevier).
49	**DOI.** [10.1016/j.nlp.2025.100179](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nlp.2025.100179) · Scopus-indexed · 2 citations · 11 references
50	
51	**Problem.** Data science literature is voluminous and fast-moving; *"Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often struggle with retrieving precisely relevant context from this dense academic corpus."*
52	
53	**Methodology.** Four coordinated stages: (1) **GROBID** structured document parsing; (2) **domain-specific embedding fine-tuning derived from textbooks**; (3) **semantic chunking** for coherence; (4) a novel **"Abstract First"** retrieval strategy prioritising *"concise, high-signal summaries."* Evaluated with **RAGAS** on a custom data-science query set, with ablations against *"configurations using only subsets of these enhancements."*
54	
55	**Results.** *"Boosts Context Relevance by over 15-fold compared to baseline RAG, surpassing configurations using only subsets of these enhancements."*
56	
57	**Advantages.** Ablation-driven; the "Abstract First" result is counter-intuitive and useful; Scopus-indexed Elsevier venue.
58	
59	**Disadvantages.** Single metric (Context Relevance only); bespoke unreleased query set, so the 15× is not independently comparable and implies a weak baseline; domain-locked by textbook-derived fine-tuning; heavy infrastructure; only 11 references and 2 citations.
60	
61	**Datasets.** Custom data-science query set (unnamed); textbook corpus for fine-tuning (unnamed). No public benchmark.
62	
63	**Relevance to ResearchGPT.** ⚠️ `RESEARCHGPT_SPEC.md §1.2` mis-describes this as "RAG-based literature assistance" — it is a retrieval-precision architecture for data science and does not generate reviews. Worse, §1.3's extension table calls it a *"Fixed single-pass pipeline"* when it is explicitly **multi-stage**. Rewrite that row: the honest contrast is **static multi-stage vs. dynamic agentic control with verification**. Also note it depends on **GROBID**, which `PROJECT_PLAN.md §2.2` cuts — a conflict you must justify if this stays your base paper. See `LITERATURE_REVIEW.md §2` for why SurveyGen (C5-17) is the better choice.

69	## C1-01 · Huang & Huang (2026) — Survey on Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation **[ABSTRACT ONLY]**
70	
71	**Citation.** Huang, Y., & Huang, J. X. (2026). *ACM Computing Surveys.* DOI [10.1145/3805774](https://doi.org/10.1145/3805774) · 34 citations · 30 references
72	
73	**Problem.** RAG has fragmented as it has grown; no shared organising vocabulary.
74	
75	**Methodology.** Organises RAG into **four sequential stages from the retrieval viewpoint: pre-retrieval → retrieval → post-retrieval → generation**, analyses significant studies per stage, then surveys evaluation methods and open challenges.
76	
77	**Advantages.** *ACM Computing Surveys* authority; the four-stage structure maps directly onto implementation; covers evaluation as well as method.
78	
79	**Disadvantages.** Survey with no new results; retrieval-centric framing under-weights agentic control — exactly where your contribution sits; only 30 references recorded, modest for CSUR.
80	
81	**Datasets.** None.
82	
83	**Relevance.** The default scaffold for your System Design chapter: Planner → pre-retrieval, Retriever → retrieval, rerank/verify → post-retrieval, Writer → generation. Borrowing a CSUR taxonomy costs nothing and makes your design instantly legible.

87	## C1-02 · Peng et al. (2025) — Graph RAG: A Survey **[ABSTRACT ONLY]**
88	
89	**Citation.** Peng, B., Zhu, Y., Liu, Y., Bo, X., Shi, H., Hong, C., Zhang, Y., & Tang, S. (2025). *ACM TOIS.* DOI [10.1145/3777378](https://doi.org/10.1145/3777378) · 66 citations
90	
91	**Problem.** Flat vector retrieval discards relational structure; *"the complex structure of relationships among different entities in databases presents challenges for RAG systems."*
92	
93	**Methodology.** First comprehensive GraphRAG survey. Formalises **Graph-Based Indexing → Graph-Guided Retrieval → Graph-Enhanced Generation**, covering core technologies, training methods, downstream tasks, evaluation, and industrial use cases. Live repository maintained.
94	
95	**Advantages.** First systematic treatment; clean three-stage formalisation; covers industrial deployments.
96	
97	**Disadvantages.** Young area (authors note its *"novelty"*); graph construction cost understated by survey framing; **no comparative benchmarking of GraphRAG vs flat RAG**, so the actual benefit is unquantified.
98	
99	**Datasets.** None.
100	
101	**Relevance.** Cite as a **deliberate non-choice**. At ~60 papers / ~3k chunks, graph indexing cost is not repaid. Naming the frontier alternative and explaining the trade-off reads as judgement; ignoring it reads as unawareness. Also your clearest Future Work item.

105	## C1-03 · Lyu et al. (2024) — CRUD-RAG **[ABSTRACT ONLY]**
106	
107	**Citation.** Lyu, Y., Li, Z., Niu, S., Xiong, F., Tang, B., Wang, W., Wu, H., Liu, H., Xu, T., & Chen, E. (2024). *ACM TOIS.* DOI [10.1145/3701228](https://doi.org/10.1145/3701228) · 88 citations
108	
109	**Problem.** RAG benchmarks *"focus primarily on question-answering applications"* and *"often assess only the LLM components of the RAG pipeline or the retriever... overlooking the impact of external knowledge base construction and the retrieval component."*
110	
111	**Methodology.** Categorises RAG applications by **CRUD**: **Create** (original varied content), **Read** (knowledge-intensive QA), **Update** (correcting inaccuracies in existing text), **Delete** (summarising long text). Separate dataset per category. Analyses the effect of *"the retriever, context length, knowledge base construction, and LLM."* Code at `github.com/IAAR-Shanghai/CRUD_RAG`.
112	
113	**Advantages.** Component-wise evaluation; covers generation scenarios beyond QA including summarisation; uniquely evaluates knowledge-base construction; public code.
114	
115	**Disadvantages.** **Chinese-language only** — the data is unusable for you; CRUD is borrowed from database semantics and fits generation loosely; no agentic or multi-step scenarios.
116	
117	**Datasets.** CRUD-RAG (own, Chinese), four sub-datasets.
118	
119	**Relevance.** Your peer-reviewed justification for **ablations 2–4**: a TOIS benchmark paper arguing that whole-pipeline evaluation hides component-level failure. Their "Delete" (long-text summarisation) is the closest published analogue to review synthesis. You can borrow the argument but not the data.

123	## C1-04 · Siriwardhana et al. (2023) — RAG-end2end ✅ FULL TEXT
124	
125	**Citation.** Siriwardhana, S., Weerasekera, R., Wen, E., Kaluarachchi, T., Rana, R., & Nanayakkara, S. (2023). *TACL* 11 (ACL Anthology `2023.tacl-1.1`). DOI [10.1162/tacl_a_00530](https://doi.org/10.1162/tacl_a_00530) · 297 citations · 59 references
126	
127	### Problem
128	RAG was only ever trained and explored on a Wikipedia knowledge base and *"is not optimized for use in other specialized domains such as healthcare and news."* Off-the-shelf RAG degrades badly on specialist corpora.
129	
130	### Methodology
131	**RAG-end2end** makes two modifications to original RAG:
132	
133	1. **Joint end-to-end training of retriever and generator**, including *"updating all components of the external knowledge base during training"* — the passage encoder, the question encoder, **and periodic re-indexing of the knowledge base** as embeddings shift. Both the passage encoder and question encoder of the DPR retriever are fine-tuned, which is what original RAG does not do.
134	2. **An auxiliary reconstruction training signal** that *"forces RAG-end2end to reconstruct a given sentence by accessing the relevant information from the external knowledge base,"* injecting domain knowledge beyond the QA objective.
135	
136	Trained for **ten epochs** per variant, selecting *"the final checkpoint with the highest validation accuracy."* Metrics: **Exact Match (EM), F1, and Top-5 / Top-20 retrieval accuracy.** Open-sourced into HuggingFace Transformers.
137	
138	### Results
139	- **Table 1: RAG-end2end-QA significantly outperforms RAG-original-QA on all metrics — EM, F1, Top-5, Top-20 — across all three domains.**
140	- EM improvements ranged **+1.13 points (News) to +12.16 points (Conversation)**.
141	- A second reported range: **+1.7 (Conversation) to +8.39 (News)**; **Top-20 retrieval accuracy up 3.2–8 points.**
142	- Reconstruction signal alone (without end2end): *"improves the performance moderately"* — EM gains **+0.84 (COVID-19) to +3.12 (Conversation)**.
143	- Highlighted single result: **13-point EM improvement in the Conversation domain.**
144	- **Table 5, SQuAD open-domain:** RAG-original **EM 28.12 / F1 39.42 / Top-5 59.64 / Top-20 72.38** → RAG-end2end **EM 40.02 / F1 52.63 / Top-5 75.79 / Top-20 85.57**. A ~12-point EM and ~13-point F1 gain.
145	- Fine-tuning DPR on its original loss with domain data also improves retrieval, but RAG-end2end *"significantly improves the DPR's domain adaptation for all three domains."*
146	
147	### Advantages
148	Large, consistent gains across three domains and on open-domain SQuAD; the auxiliary reconstruction objective is elegant and reusable; strong evidence that **a domain-specific retriever is the key driver** — the authors *"argue... that when adapting RAG to various domains, having a domain-specific retriever plays a key role"*; shipped in HuggingFace Transformers, unusually strong reproducibility evidence.
149	
150	### Disadvantages
151	Requires **full end-to-end training with periodic knowledge-base re-encoding** — very heavy. Their own stated failure mode: *"If the knowledge base is not entirely updated with the new embeddings, the re-indexing process fails."* Restricted to open-domain QA, not long-form generation. Pre-dates instruction-tuned LLMs, so baselines are dated.
152	
153	### Datasets
154	**COVID-19** (CORD-19), **News**, **Conversations**; plus **SQuAD** open-domain. Also references Natural Questions and TriviaQA. Models: DPR, BART, BERT, BM25.
155	
156	### Relevance to ResearchGPT
157	This is your **defence for a frozen retriever**. It is the strongest evidence that joint retriever–generator training is the most effective domain-adaptation route, and it is flatly infeasible at $0 on CPU. Naming the superior method you rejected, with the reason, converts a resource limit into a scope decision.
158	
159	It also sharpens your **trained verifier's** contribution: you adapt the *verification* component to the domain instead of the retriever — the cheap end of the same idea. And their re-indexing failure mode is a concrete argument for why your frozen `bge-small` index is operationally simpler, not merely cheaper. Put this in both Limitations and Future Work.
160

163	# C2 — AGENTIC & SELF-REFLECTIVE RAG
164	
165	## C2-05 · Jeong et al. (2024) — Adaptive-RAG ✅ FULL TEXT
166	
167	**Citation.** Jeong, S., Baek, J., Cho, S., Hwang, S. J., & Park, J. C. (2024). *NAACL-HLT 2024*, pp. 7036–7050. KAIST. DOI [10.18653/v1/2024.naacl-long.389](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2024.naacl-long.389) · 182 citations
168	
169	### Problem
170	Existing retrieval strategies *"either handle simple queries with unnecessary computational overhead or fail to adequately address complex multi-step queries; yet, not all user requests fall into only one of the simple or complex categories."*
171	
172	The paper's framing question is worth quoting: *"In a real-world scenario, are all the requests from users complex? Instead, users might often ask simple and straightforward questions, while only occasionally asking complex ones."* They also critique existing adaptive methods directly — entity-frequency approaches *"are overly simplistic, failing to consider multi-hop queries,"* while multi-step-output approaches are *"excessively complex, terminating answer solving steps after several rounds of module access."*
173	
174	### Methodology
175	Three strategies selected per query by a classifier (Figure 2 in the paper):
176	
177	- **(A) No retrieval** — for straightforward queries answerable from parametric memory ("Paris is the capital of what?").
178	- **(B) Single-step retrieval** — one retrieval, then answer.
179	- **(C) Multi-step / iterative retrieval** — repeated retrieval and intermediate answers, *k* times.
180	
181	The **complexity classifier is a smaller LM** trained to predict complexity level. Its training data is built **without human labelling**, via two strategies: (i) **predicted outcomes** — which models actually answer which queries correctly; and (ii) **inherent dataset bias** — *"samples in the datasets are designed either for single-step or for multi-step QA scenarios."* Classifier training queries do not overlap with test queries.
182	
183	Metrics: **F1, EM, and Accuracy (Acc)** where *"Acc measures whether the predicted answer contains the ground-truth answer"*; plus **Time per Query** and **Step** count for efficiency.
184	
185	### Results
186	- Figure 1 plots **F1 (47–51 range) against Time per Query (0.5–3.5s)** with GPT-3.5-Turbo-Instruct, showing Adaptive-RAG dominating the efficiency/accuracy frontier versus No Retrieval, Single-step, Adaptive Retrieval, and Multi-step.
187	- *"The classification accuracy of our Adaptive-RAG is better than those of the other adaptive retrieval baselines, which leads to overall QA performance improvements."*
188	- **Classifier ablation (their table):** Adaptive-RAG **F1 46.94, Step 1084**, with per-class accuracy All 54.52 / No 30.52 / One 66.28 / Multi 65.45. **w/o Binary:** F1 43.43, Step 640. **w/o Silver:** F1 48.79, Step 1464 — higher F1 but **35% more steps**, and No-retrieval accuracy collapses to 0.00.
189	- An **oracle classifier** *"achieves the best performance while being much more efficient"* than the trained classifier — quantifying the headroom.
190	- Classifier size ablation: *"no significant performance differences among classifiers of various sizes, even with reduced complexity and fewer parameters in smaller classifiers."*
191	
192	### Advantages
193	Improves **both** efficiency and accuracy rather than trading them; automatic label collection removes the annotation bottleneck; **smaller classifiers work as well as larger ones**, so routing is genuinely cheap; validated on GPT-3.5 and FLAN-T5 series; beats other adaptive-retrieval baselines, not just static RAG.
194	
195	### Disadvantages (their own Limitations, verbatim highlights)
196	*"As there are no available datasets for training the query-complexity classifier, we automatically create new data based on the model prediction outcomes and the inductive dataset biases. However, our labeling process is one specific instantiation of labeling the query complexity, and it may have the potential to label queries incorrectly despite its effectiveness."*
197	
198	And on the oracle gap: *"as the performance gap between the ideal classifier in Table 1 and the current classifier in Figure 3 indicates, there is still room to improve the effectiveness of the classifier."* They describe their design as *"the initial, simplest instantiation."*
199	
200	### Datasets
201	Single-hop: **SQuAD, Natural Questions, TriviaQA**. Multi-hop: **MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA**. Models: GPT-3.5, FLAN-T5 series, T5-based classifier, BM25 retriever.
202	
203	### Relevance to ResearchGPT
204	**The strongest published precedent for your Planner**, with three concrete transfers:
205	
206	1. **Design justification.** "One retrieval strategy does not fit all sub-questions" is not your assumption — it is their empirically supported thesis, at a NAACL main track with 182 citations.
207	2. **A cheaper Planner.** Their finding that **small classifiers match large ones** is directly actionable: under your rate-limited free tier, routing sub-questions with a small *local* classifier instead of an API call would cut request volume with no measured loss.
208	3. **Expect the router to be your bottleneck.** They state it themselves — the oracle-vs-trained gap is the dominant error source. If you build routing logic, instrument it and report its accuracy separately.
209	
210	**The architectural contrast that sharpens your contribution:** Adaptive-RAG routes **once, before retrieval, on the query alone**. Your Critic re-routes **after seeing what came back**. That is a real difference and it is `LITERATURE_REVIEW.md §5 Gap 3`.

214	## C2-06 · Yu et al. (2024) — Chain-of-Note ✅ FULL TEXT
215	
216	**Citation.** Yu, W., Zhang, H., Pan, X., Cao, P., Ma, K., Li, J., Wang, H., & Yu, D. (2024). *EMNLP 2024*, p. 14679. DOI [10.18653/v1/2024.emnlp-main.813](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2024.emnlp-main.813) · 41 citations
217	
218	### Problem
219	Two distinct failure modes: *"the reliability of the retrieved information is not always guaranteed, and the retrieval of irrelevant data can mislead the response generation"*; and *"standard RALMs frequently neglect their intrinsic knowledge due to the interference from retrieved information."* Desired behaviour: use intrinsic knowledge when retrieval is poor, and *"in the absence of both intrinsic and retrieved knowledge, opt to respond with 'unknown' to avoid hallucination."*
220	
221	### Methodology
222	**CHAIN-OF-NOTE (CON)** generates *"sequential reading notes for each retrieved document,"* assessing each document's relevance before integrating anything. Two deployment modes: (a) prompting GPT-4 with CON; (b) distillation — *"we utilized GPT-4 to create 10K CON data, subsequently trained on LLaMa-2 7B model."*
223	
224	Metrics: **EM** (normalised per Karpukhin et al.) and **F1** for open-domain QA; **Rejection Rate (RR)** for unanswerable/real-time questions. GPT-4 is scored with **Accuracy rather than EM**, because *"since GPT-4 is not directly trained on open-domain QA benchmarks, employing EM / F1 for evaluation is challenging."*
225	
226	### Results
227	- **+7.9 EM** on fully noisy documents, averaged across three open-domain QA datasets.
228	- **+10.5 increase in rejection rate** for real-time questions beyond the pre-training knowledge scope.
229	- **+1.97 average EM** across all three datasets using **LLaMa-2** as backbone.
230	- **Table 4 (RealTimeQA, unknown robustness):** Retrieve-Read **EM 15.6 / F1 19.9 / RR 6.1** → + CHAIN-OF-NOTE **EM 15.7 / F1 20.3 / RR 13.0**. Note the RR **more than doubles** while EM/F1 barely move — the gain is almost entirely *knowing when to refuse*.
231	- GPT-4 with CON outperforms chain-of-thought prompting.
232	- Improvement *"varies depending on whether DPR successfully retrieves relevant documents."*
233	
234	### Advantages
235	Explicit, measurable **refusal capability** — rare in this literature; distillation into a 7B model works; per-document notes are inherently interpretable; robustness gains under noisy retrieval are the largest reported effect.
236	
237	### Disadvantages (their Limitations, verbatim)
238	*"One major limitation of the CHAIN-OF-NOTE (CON) approach is its increased inference cost due to the sequential generation of notes. While CON is beneficial for assessing the relevance and integrating external knowledge, it results in longer response times, which is problematic for time-sensitive applications. Moreover, the system's efficiency depends on the conciseness and relevance of the generated notes, which can fluctuate based on the complexity of the retrieved documents."*
239	
240	Also: distillation requires GPT-4 access; the four benchmarks are not all named in-text; note quality is itself unverified LLM output.
241	
242	### Datasets
243	**TriviaQA** and **RealTimeQA** named explicitly; three open-domain QA datasets for the main results plus a fourth for fine-tuning experiments. 10K GPT-4-generated CON training set. Models: GPT-4, LLaMa-2 7B, DPR.
244	
245	### Relevance to ResearchGPT
246	**The intellectual precedent for your hallucination stress test** (`PROJECT_PLAN.md §9.5`), and the RealTimeQA result is the template: RR **6.1 → 13.0** while EM barely moves. That is exactly the shape of result your stress test should produce — *the system refuses more, without getting worse at what it can answer*. Report it the same way.
247	
248	**But read the limitation as a budget warning.** Sequential note generation is one LLM call per retrieved document. With top-12 chunks per sub-question across 4–8 sub-questions, CON would be hundreds of extra calls per run — impossible on a rate-limited free tier. Your **local NLI verifier is the cost-appropriate substitute**: same goal (filter unreliable retrieved content before it reaches the output), radically cheaper mechanism, and unlike CON's notes it is independently auditable. Make that comparison explicitly in your Design chapter — it shows you understood the technique and chose deliberately.

252	## C2-07 · Jeong et al. (2024) — Self-BioRAG **[ABSTRACT ONLY]**
253	
254	**Citation.** Jeong, M., Sohn, J., Sung, M., & Kang, J. (2024). *Bioinformatics* 40(Suppl 1). DOI [10.1093/bioinformatics/btae238](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btae238) · 115 citations
255	
256	**Problem.** *"When applying existing methods to different domain-specific problems, poor generalization becomes apparent, leading to fetching incorrect documents or making inaccurate judgments."*
257	
258	**Methodology.** **Self-BioRAG** specialises in *"generating explanations, retrieving domain-specific documents, and self-reflecting generated responses."* Trained on **84k filtered biomedical instruction sets** so the model *"can assess its generated explanations with customized reflective tokens"* — reflection is a learned in-model behaviour, not an external check. Weights (7B, 13B), data and code released at `github.com/dmis-lab/self-biorag`.
259	
260	**Results.** **+7.2% absolute average improvement** over the state-of-the-art open foundation model at ≤7B parameters, across three medical QA benchmarks. **+8% ROUGE-1 over RAG** on two long-form QA benchmarks.
261	
262	**Advantages.** The long-form QA gain matters most for you — closer to review writing than multiple-choice. Full artefact release. Demonstrates domain-specific retriever + corpus + instructions are *jointly* necessary.
263	
264	**Disadvantages.** Requires 84k domain instructions you cannot construct at $0; biomedical only; **reflection is internal to the model, so its judgements cannot be independently audited**; 7B inference impractical on CPU.
265	
266	**Datasets.** 84k biomedical instruction sets; three medical QA benchmarks and two long-form QA benchmarks (not named in abstract).
267	
268	**Relevance.** Peer-reviewed evidence that self-reflection improves RAG, *and that the gain holds for long-form output*. But the more important reading is the contrast: Self-BioRAG bakes reflection into the model; you externalise it into a separate trained verifier. **That is arguably the better design for your purpose — an external verifier can be ablated, audited and reported on; reflective tokens cannot be separated from the generator.** This is the argument that justifies ablation 2 as your headline experiment.

274	**Citation.** Li, Y., Ke, W., Liu, J., Wang, P., Liu, J., & He, Y. (2025). *Information Processing & Management.* DOI [10.1016/j.ipm.2025.104369](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ipm.2025.104369) · 10 citations · 43 references

277	The **bibliographic record is verified** in OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar (DOI, title, six authors, journal, 43 references). But **no abstract exists in OpenAlex, Crossref or Semantic Scholar**, and ScienceDirect returns **HTTP 403** to automated access. There is a **year discrepancy**: OpenAlex says 2025, Semantic Scholar says 2026.

287	## C2-09 · Ammann, Golde & Akbik (2025) — Question Decomposition for RAG ✅ FULL TEXT
288	
289	**Citation.** Ammann, P., Golde, J., & Akbik, A. (2025). *ACL 2025: Student Research Workshop*, p. 501. Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin. DOI [10.18653/v1/2025.acl-srw.32](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.acl-srw.32) · 9 citations
290	
291	### Problem
292	Multi-hop questions defeat standard RAG because *"relevant facts are often distributed across multiple documents rather than co-occurring in one source."* Semantic similarity to the whole question retrieves no single passage that answers it.
293	
294	### Methodology
295	Three stages: **(i)** an LLM decomposes the query into sub-questions; **(ii)** passages retrieved per sub-question; **(iii)** *"the merged candidate pool is reranked."* A filtering step retains *"only passages that clearly address distinct aspects of the original question, improving precision in the final evidence set."*
296	
297	Four configurations compared: **Naive RAG**, **QD** (decomposition only), **RR** (reranking only), **QD+RR** (both). Generation with **Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct** in bfloat16, temperature 0.8, nucleus sampling top-p 0.8. Metrics: **Hits@4, Hits@10, MAP@10, MRR@10** for retrieval; **F1, EM, precision, recall** plus supporting-fact and joint metrics for answers. Code released.
298	
299	The authors are explicit about novelty: *"Although reranking itself is standard, we show that pairing an off-the-shelf cross-encoder reranker with LLM-driven question decomposition bridges the retrieval gap on multi-hop questions and provides a practical, drop-in enhancement, without any extra training or specialized indexing."*
300	
301	### Results
302	**MultiHop-RAG (retrieval):**
303	- **QD alone:** +4.4 points Hits@4, +2.9 Hits@10.
304	- **RR alone:** +7.6 points Hits@4; *"substantially improves MAP@10 and MRR@10."*
305	- **QD+RR:** best overall — **87.2% Hits@10 and 0.635 MRR@10**.
306	- Against the dataset's published baseline (**74.7% Hits@10, 0.586 MRR@10**): *"our QD+RR thus improves Hits@10 by 16.5% and MRR@10 by 8.4%"* — **achieved "despite using a smaller embedding model."**
307	- MAP@10 rises to 0.322 with QD+RR vs 0.274 for RR alone, *"suggesting that reranking not only filters noise but leverages the broader context to prioritize relevant passages."*
308	
309	**HotpotQA dev (Table 2):**
310	
311	| System | F1 | P | R | EM |
312	|---|---|---|---|---|
313	| Naive RAG | 31.3 | 33.1 | 31.2 | 25.4 |
314	| QD | 32.3 | 34.3 | 32.0 | 26.1 |
315	| RR | 32.9 | 35.0 | 32.7 | 26.4 |
316	| **QD+RR** | **35.0** | **37.1** | **34.8** | **28.1** |
317	
318	Supporting-fact metrics: Naive 18.4/12.0/42.8 · QD 17.0/10.6/44.1 · RR **19.6**/**12.9**/44.9 · QD+RR 17.9/11.2/**46.8**. Joint: Naive 8.7/5.9/20.2 · QD 8.0/5.2/20.7 · RR **9.5**/**6.4**/21.4 · QD+RR 8.9/5.8/**23.1**.
319	
320	Note the nuance: **QD+RR wins on precision (46.8 supporting-fact, 23.1 joint) but RR alone wins on supporting-fact EM/F1** — decomposition trades some exactness for coverage. Their summary: *"the former improves coverage, while the latter restores precision."*
321	
322	**Ablation:** comparing sub-query count to gold evidence count, *"both Pearson and Spearman coefficients are near zero... indicating no correlation"* — the decomposer does not learn how many hops a question actually needs.
323	
324	### Advantages
325	Large retrieval gains with **no training and no specialised indexing**; two public named benchmarks; genuinely careful about which component contributes what; unusually honest about its own novelty.
326	
327	### Disadvantages (their Limitations, verbatim — all six)
328	1. **Single-hop and adverse cases.** *"Question decomposition can be counterproductive when the original query is already specific. In such cases, subqueries may introduce noise or distract from the original intent."*
329	2. **Prompt and model sensitivity.** *"The quality of subqueries is sensitive to both the prompt design and the underlying LLM."*
330	3. **Computational overhead.** *"Generating M subqueries and reranking M × k candidate passages substantially increases latency and GPU requirements."*
331	4. **Pipeline complexity.** *"Every extra component increases engineering overhead, latency, and potential points of failure."*
332	5. **Reranker and domain dependence.** *"The observed gains rely on a strong, domain-aligned cross-encoder reranker. When the reranker is mismatched with the retrieval or task domain, the benefits of decomposition may diminish or vanish entirely."*
333	6. **Lack of iterative retrieval.** *"Our pipeline operates in a single-shot manner: subqueries are generated once and not updated based on retrieved evidence. This limits its ability to support adaptive multi-step reasoning."*
334	
335	Plus: SRW venue (lighter review), 9 citations.
336	
337	### Datasets
338	**MultiHop-RAG** and **HotpotQA**. Model: Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct.
339	
340	### Relevance to ResearchGPT
341	**Your single closest methodological relative — and now, after reading the full text, also your best Introduction quote.**
342	
343	**Their limitation #6 is your contribution.** *"Subqueries are generated once and not updated based on retrieved evidence"* is precisely what your Critic loop fixes: your Critic sees retrieval results, assesses coverage, and sends control back to the Planner or Retriever. Quote it verbatim, cite it, and your bounded feedback loop stops being a design preference and becomes a documented open problem you address.
344	
345	**Their limitation #5 is a warning you must act on.** *"The observed gains rely on a strong, domain-aligned cross-encoder reranker"* — and `PROJECT_PLAN.md §6.1` downgrades your reranker to a **22M MiniLM** for CPU speed, which is neither strong nor domain-aligned. Their gains may not replicate at your model scale. Two responses: measure reranking's contribution separately on Day 4, and treat the cut §4.3 reranker fine-tune as the mitigation if the measured gain is poor.
346	
347	**Three more transfers:**
348	- **A Day-5 sanity check.** Decomposition + reranking should yield a large retrieval gain. If yours is far below their +16.5% Hits@10, suspect a bug rather than a finding.
349	- **It bounds your novelty, usefully.** Query decomposition + reranking is published and quantified. Your contribution is what happens *after*: structured extraction, verification, the loop. Being precise here makes your claims more credible.
350	- **A better ablation-4 baseline.** "Decomposition + rerank, no verification, no loop" is a competitive published configuration — far stronger than a vanilla-RAG strawman.

356	## C3-10 · Qian et al. (2024) — ChatDev ✅ FULL TEXT

358	**Citation.** Qian, C., Liu, W., Liu, H., Chen, N., Dang, Y., Li, J., Yang, C., Chen, W., Su, Y., Cong, X., Xu, J., Li, D., Liu, Z., & Sun, M. (2024). *ACL 2024 (Long Papers)*. Tsinghua University. DOI [10.18653/v1/2024.acl-long.810](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2024.acl-long.810) · 279 citations (OpenAlex) / 1,043 (Semantic Scholar)
359	
360	### Problem
361	Phase-specific models fragment multi-stage workflows: *"the deep learning model in each phase requires unique designs, leading to technical inconsistencies across various phases, which results in a fragmented and ineffective development process."*
362	
363	### Methodology
364	**ChatDev** is *"a chat-powered software-development framework integrating multiple 'software agents' for active involvement in three core phases of the software lifecycle: design, coding, and testing."* Two named control mechanisms:
365	
366	- **Chat chain** — governs *what* agents communicate; structures the sequence of agent interactions.
367	- **Communicative dehallucination** — governs *how* they communicate. It *"encourages the assistant to actively seek more detailed suggestions from the instructor before delivering a formal response."* Note the mechanism: hallucination is reduced by making the receiving agent **ask for clarification before committing**, rather than by checking output afterwards.
368	
369	A reported qualitative finding: natural language suits system design, while programming language suits debugging — the communication medium should match the sub-task.
370	
371	Evaluation dimensions: **completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality**.
372	
373	### Advantages
374	The canonical peer-reviewed demonstration that role specialisation with structured communication beats monolithic prompting. **Communicative dehallucination explicitly recognises that multi-agent systems create new hallucination surfaces at agent interfaces** — a failure mode most multi-agent papers ignore entirely. Very high citation count; ACL long paper.
375	
376	### Disadvantages (their Limitations, verbatim highlights)
377	- *"The capabilities of autonomous agents in software production might be overestimated. While they enhance development quality, agents often implement simple logic, resulting in low information density. Without clear, detailed requirements, agents struggle to grasp task ideas."*
378	- *"Currently, these technologies are more suitable for prototype systems rather than complex real-world applications."*
379	- *"Automating the evaluation of general-purpose software is highly complex... manual verification for large datasets is impractical."*
380	- *"Compared to single-agent approaches, multiple agents require more tokens and time, increasing computational demands and environmental impact. Future research should aim to enhance agent capabilities with fewer interactions."*
381	
382	Plus: software-engineering domain with no retrieval or evidence grounding; **no quantitative results extractable from the main text** — the paper's contribution is architectural and qualitative.
383	
384	### Datasets
385	**None** — evaluated on software-development tasks, not a public benchmark. Models: ChatGPT, GPT-4.
386	
387	### Relevance to ResearchGPT
388	**Your primary citation for "role decomposition works,"** and the answer to "why not one big prompt?"
389	
390	But the more valuable transfer is **communicative dehallucination**. ChatDev found multi-agent systems hallucinate *at agent boundaries* — one agent's imprecise output becomes another's confident input. Your pipeline has five such handoffs (Planner→Retriever→Extractor→Verifier→Critic→Writer) and errors compound along them. `RESEARCHGPT_SPEC.md` addresses grounding of the *final output* but never inter-agent drift. Two consequences:
391	
392	- **Your Verifier already mitigates this by construction** — it re-grounds Extractor output against source chunks, breaking the drift chain mid-pipeline. Claim that explicitly; it is a design strength currently unstated.
393	- **Your `trace.jsonl` is the instrument to measure it.** Logging per-agent input/output as the spec requires lets you actually observe boundary drift — a cheap, interesting minor finding.
394	
395	Their token-cost admission (*"multiple agents require more tokens and time"*) is also the honest framing for your own cost table — pair it with AutoHMA-LLM (C3-12), which shows tiered model assignment can *reduce* cost.
396	
397	---

399	## C3-11 · Li et al. (2024) — Survey on LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems ✅ FULL TEXT
400	
401	**Citation.** Li, X., Wang, S., Zeng, S., Wu, Y., & Yang, Y. (2024). *Vicinagearth* 1(9). Wuhan University / Zhejiang University. DOI [10.1007/s44336-024-00009-2](https://doi.org/10.1007/s44336-024-00009-2) · 307 citations · **254 references** · 43 pages
402	
403	### Problem
404	LLM-based multi-agent systems have proliferated without a unifying account, making architectures hard to compare.
405	
406	### Methodology
407	Systematic survey synthesising **five key components: profile, perception, self-action, mutual interaction, and evolution**. The **self-action** module is decomposed further, including a **memory** module — *"serving as the storage and recall unit for the agent... instrumental in allowing it to leverage existing cognitive and experiential knowledge to adapt to dynamic interactions with the environment or other agents."* Applications split into **problem-solving** and **world simulation**.
408	
409	### Content relevant to your system
410	The survey's treatment of **hallucination mitigation in multi-agent settings** is the most useful part:
411	
412	- It distinguishes **intrinsic hallucinations** (*"text generation that contradicts input logic"*) from **extrinsic hallucinations** (*"text generation containing information that cannot be verified with existing information"*). Your Verifier targets the extrinsic kind.
413	- Mitigation families it catalogues: *"integrate external knowledge bases and fact-checking systems to verify the accuracy of generated content"*; **RAG** methods that provide *"mechanisms to check for inconsistencies between the generated response and the source material"*; and **decoding strategies** that balance *"diversity and factual accuracy."*
414	- **CoVe** is described as a direct analogue of your design: it *"encourages models to generate initial responses, followed by verification queries to check the draft's factual accuracy before producing a refined response."*
415	- **Multi-agent debate** for factuality: *"deploys multiple instances of LLMs in debates to achieve consensus, thereby enhancing reasoning and factual accuracy"*; **ChatEval** *"simulates the collective wisdom and cognitive collaboration of human evaluators by constructing a multi-agent debate system."*
416	- **Plan revision on failure** — DEPS-style systems where *"agents initiate action planning for a specific task and proceed with execution unless indications of plan failure emerge during the process,"* and prerequisite errors *"prompt the LLM to revise the plan accordingly."* This is the closest published description of your Critic→Planner edge.
417	- **Reflection on past failures** — Retroformer *"enables an agent to reflect on its past failures, integrating these reflections into prompts to guide future actions."*
418	
419	### Advantages
420	254 references — genuinely comprehensive; the five-component framework gives standard vocabulary; 307 citations despite a young venue; the problem-solving vs. world-simulation split cleanly locates your system.
421	
422	### Disadvantages
423	Survey with no evaluation or empirical comparison. The five components are **descriptive rather than prescriptive** — they classify systems without predicting which designs work. General MAS framing with no document- or retrieval-specific content. It also flags a structural risk that applies to you: centralised designs are *"susceptible to single points of failure and communication delays"* — in your graph, the Critic is that central point.

425	⚠️ **Venue caution.** *Vicinagearth* launched in 2024. **Verify it is Scopus-indexed before relying on it in a Scopus-constrained bibliography.** If not, substitute **Wang et al. (2024), *Frontiers of Computer Science*, [10.1007/s11704-024-40231-1](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11704-024-40231-1)** — 1,320 citations, established venue.
426	
427	### Datasets
428	**None** — survey. Models discussed: GPT-3/3.5/4, ChatGPT, LLaMA, Llama2, PaLM, BERT.
429	
430	### Relevance to ResearchGPT
431	Use it to **describe your architecture in the field's own vocabulary**, and note honestly where you don't fit: four of the five components map cleanly onto your system, but **"evolution" does not** — your agents don't learn across runs. Your adaptation is *within-run* (the Critic loop). Naming that gap reads as rigour and gives you a clean Future Work item.
432	
433	The DEPS description (plan revision when *"indications of plan failure emerge"*) and CoVe (*"verification queries to check the draft's factual accuracy before producing a refined response"*) are the two closest published analogues to your Critic and Verifier respectively. Cite both — they show your design pattern is recognised, while neither has been applied to literature review.

438	
439	**Citation.** Yang, T., Feng, P., Guo, Q., Zhang, J., Zhang, X., Ning, J., Wang, X., & Mao, Z. (2025). *IEEE Transactions on Cognitive Communications and Networking.* DOI [10.1109/tccn.2025.3528892](https://doi.org/10.1109/tccn.2025.3528892) · 38 citations

# Full-Text Deep Dive — 25 Papers + Base Paper

> **What this is.** An extensive summary of *what is actually inside each paper* — architecture details, experimental setup, every reported number, ablations, and the authors' own verbatim limitations. This goes beyond `PAPER_ANALYSIS.md`, which was written from abstracts.
>
> **How the papers were obtained.** PDFs downloaded from ACL Anthology, Springer, Nature and BMC; full text for two paywalled biomedical papers retrieved from **Europe PMC** (`PMC11231046`, `PMC10919922`); TACL located on ACL Anthology (`2023.tacl-1.1`). Text extracted with PyMuPDF, reference lists trimmed.
>
> ### ⚠️ Coverage — read this first
>
> **18 of 26 papers were obtained in full text.** The remaining **8 are abstract-only** because the publisher blocked automated access (HTTP 403) or the paper is paywalled with no OA route:
>
> | Abstract-only | Reason |
> |---|---|
> | **BASE** Aytar et al. | Elsevier, no OA |
> | **C1-01** Huang & Huang (ACM CSUR) | ACM DL 403 |
> | **C1-02** Peng et al. (ACM TOIS) | ACM DL 403 |
> | **C1-03** Lyu et al. (ACM TOIS) | ACM DL 403 |
> | **C2-07** Jeong et al. (Bioinformatics) | OUP 403; not OA in Europe PMC |
> | **C2-08** Li et al. (IP&M) | Elsevier, **no abstract anywhere** |
> | **C3-12** Yang et al. (IEEE TCCN) | IEEE paywall |
> | **C6-24** Huang et al. (ACM TOIS) | ACM DL 403 |
>
> Entries for those 8 are explicitly marked **[ABSTRACT ONLY]** and are necessarily thinner. Everything else below is from the full paper. Sections labelled **"Relevance to ResearchGPT"** are my analysis; everything else is the paper's own content.
>
> *Compiled 2026-08-06. Companion to `LITERATURE_REVIEW.md` and `PAPER_ANALYSIS.md`.*

---

## The five most important things the full texts revealed

These did not appear in any abstract and change decisions in `PROJECT_PLAN.md`.

## C1-04 · Siriwardhana et al. (2023) — RAG-end2end ✅ FULL TEXT

**Citation.** Siriwardhana, S., Weerasekera, R., Wen, E., Kaluarachchi, T., Rana, R., & Nanayakkara, S. (2023). *TACL* 11 (ACL Anthology `2023.tacl-1.1`). DOI [10.1162/tacl_a_00530](https://doi.org/10.1162/tacl_a_00530) · 297 citations · 59 references

### Problem
RAG was only ever trained and explored on a Wikipedia knowledge base and *"is not optimized for use in other specialized domains such as healthcare and news."* Off-the-shelf RAG degrades badly on specialist corpora.

### Methodology
**RAG-end2end** makes two modifications to original RAG:

1. **Joint end-to-end training of retriever and generator**, including *"updating all components of the external knowledge base during training"* — the passage encoder, the question encoder, **and periodic re-indexing of the knowledge base** as embeddings shift. Both the passage encoder and question encoder of the DPR retriever are fine-tuned, which is what original RAG does not do.
2. **An auxiliary reconstruction training signal** that *"forces RAG-end2end to reconstruct a given sentence by accessing the relevant information from the external knowledge base,"* injecting domain knowledge beyond the QA objective.

Trained for **ten epochs** per variant, selecting *"the final checkpoint with the highest validation accuracy."* Metrics: **Exact Match (EM), F1, and Top-5 / Top-20 retrieval accuracy.** Open-sourced into HuggingFace Transformers.

### Results
- **Table 1: RAG-end2end-QA significantly outperforms RAG-original-QA on all metrics — EM, F1, Top-5, Top-20 — across all three domains.**
- EM improvements ranged **+1.13 points (News) to +12.16 points (Conversation)**.
- A second reported range: **+1.7 (Conversation) to +8.39 (News)**; **Top-20 retrieval accuracy up 3.2–8 points.**
- Reconstruction signal alone (without end2end): *"improves the performance moderately"* — EM gains **+0.84 (COVID-19) to +3.12 (Conversation)**.
- Highlighted single result: **13-point EM improvement in the Conversation domain.**
- **Table 5, SQuAD open-domain:** RAG-original **EM 28.12 / F1 39.42 / Top-5 59.64 / Top-20 72.38** → RAG-end2end **EM 40.02 / F1 52.63 / Top-5 75.79 / Top-20 85.57**. A ~12-point EM and ~13-point F1 gain.
- Fine-tuning DPR on its original loss with domain data also improves retrieval, but RAG-end2end *"significantly improves the DPR's domain adaptation for all three domains."*

### Advantages
Large, consistent gains across three domains and on open-domain SQuAD; the auxiliary reconstruction objective is elegant and reusable; strong evidence that **a domain-specific retriever is the key driver** — the authors *"argue... that when adapting RAG to various domains, having a domain-specific retriever plays a key role"*; shipped in HuggingFace Transformers, unusually strong reproducibility evidence.

### Disadvantages
Requires **full end-to-end training with periodic knowledge-base re-encoding** — very heavy. Their own stated failure mode: *"If the knowledge base is not entirely updated with the new embeddings, the re-indexing process fails."* Restricted to open-domain QA, not long-form generation. Pre-dates instruction-tuned LLMs, so baselines are dated.

### Datasets
**COVID-19** (CORD-19), **News**, **Conversations**; plus **SQuAD** open-domain. Also references Natural Questions and TriviaQA. Models: DPR, BART, BERT, BM25.

### Relevance to ResearchGPT
This is your **defence for a frozen retriever**. It is the strongest evidence that joint retriever–generator training is the most effective domain-adaptation route, and it is flatly infeasible at $0 on CPU. Naming the superior method you rejected, with the reason, converts a resource limit into a scope decision.

It also sharpens your **trained verifier's** contribution: you adapt the *verification* component to the domain instead of the retriever — the cheap end of the same idea. And their re-indexing failure mode is a concrete argument for why your frozen `bge-small` index is operationally simpler, not merely cheaper. Put this in both Limitations and Future Work.

## C2-05 · Jeong et al. (2024) — Adaptive-RAG ✅ FULL TEXT

**Citation.** Jeong, S., Baek, J., Cho, S., Hwang, S. J., & Park, J. C. (2024). *NAACL-HLT 2024*, pp. 7036–7050. KAIST. DOI [10.18653/v1/2024.naacl-long.389](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2024.naacl-long.389) · 182 citations

### Problem
Existing retrieval strategies *"either handle simple queries with unnecessary computational overhead or fail to adequately address complex multi-step queries; yet, not all user requests fall into only one of the simple or complex categories."*

The paper's framing question is worth quoting: *"In a real-world scenario, are all the requests from users complex? Instead, users might often ask simple and straightforward questions, while only occasionally asking complex ones."* They also critique existing adaptive methods directly — entity-frequency approaches *"are overly simplistic, failing to consider multi-hop queries,"* while multi-step-output approaches are *"excessively complex, terminating answer solving steps after several rounds of module access."*

### Methodology
Three strategies selected per query by a classifier (Figure 2 in the paper):

- **(A) No retrieval** — for straightforward queries answerable from parametric memory ("Paris is the capital of what?").
- **(B) Single-step retrieval** — one retrieval, then answer.
- **(C) Multi-step / iterative retrieval** — repeated retrieval and intermediate answers, *k* times.

The **complexity classifier is a smaller LM** trained to predict complexity level. Its training data is built **without human labelling**, via two strategies: (i) **predicted outcomes** — which models actually answer which queries correctly; and (ii) **inherent dataset bias** — *"samples in the datasets are designed either for single-step or for multi-step QA scenarios."* Classifier training queries do not overlap with test queries.

Metrics: **F1, EM, and Accuracy (Acc)** where *"Acc measures whether the predicted answer contains the ground-truth answer"*; plus **Time per Query** and **Step** count for efficiency.

### Results
- Figure 1 plots **F1 (47–51 range) against Time per Query (0.5–3.5s)** with GPT-3.5-Turbo-Instruct, showing Adaptive-RAG dominating the efficiency/accuracy frontier versus No Retrieval, Single-step, Adaptive Retrieval, and Multi-step.
- *"The classification accuracy of our Adaptive-RAG is better than those of the other adaptive retrieval baselines, which leads to overall QA performance improvements."*
- **Classifier ablation (their table):** Adaptive-RAG **F1 46.94, Step 1084**, with per-class accuracy All 54.52 / No 30.52 / One 66.28 / Multi 65.45. **w/o Binary:** F1 43.43, Step 640. **w/o Silver:** F1 48.79, Step 1464 — higher F1 but **35% more steps**, and No-retrieval accuracy collapses to 0.00.
- An **oracle classifier** *"achieves the best performance while being much more efficient"* than the trained classifier — quantifying the headroom.
- Classifier size ablation: *"no significant performance differences among classifiers of various sizes, even with reduced complexity and fewer parameters in smaller classifiers."*

### Advantages
Improves **both** efficiency and accuracy rather than trading them; automatic label collection removes the annotation bottleneck; **smaller classifiers work as well as larger ones**, so routing is genuinely cheap; validated on GPT-3.5 and FLAN-T5 series; beats other adaptive-retrieval baselines, not just static RAG.

### Disadvantages (their own Limitations, verbatim highlights)
*"As there are no available datasets for training the query-complexity classifier, we automatically create new data based on the model prediction outcomes and the inductive dataset biases. However, our labeling process is one specific instantiation of labeling the query complexity, and it may have the potential to label queries incorrectly despite its effectiveness."*

And on the oracle gap: *"as the performance gap between the ideal classifier in Table 1 and the current classifier in Figure 3 indicates, there is still room to improve the effectiveness of the classifier."* They describe their design as *"the initial, simplest instantiation."*

### Datasets
Single-hop: **SQuAD, Natural Questions, TriviaQA**. Multi-hop: **MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA**. Models: GPT-3.5, FLAN-T5 series, T5-based classifier, BM25 retriever.

### Relevance to ResearchGPT
**The strongest published precedent for your Planner**, with three concrete transfers:

1. **Design justification.** "One retrieval strategy does not fit all sub-questions" is not your assumption — it is their empirically supported thesis, at a NAACL main track with 182 citations.
2. **A cheaper Planner.** Their finding that **small classifiers match large ones** is directly actionable: under your rate-limited free tier, routing sub-questions with a small *local* classifier instead of an API call would cut request volume with no measured loss.
3. **Expect the router to be your bottleneck.** They state it themselves — the oracle-vs-trained gap is the dominant error source. If you build routing logic, instrument it and report its accuracy separately.

**The architectural contrast that sharpens your contribution:** Adaptive-RAG routes **once, before retrieval, on the query alone**. Your Critic re-routes **after seeing what came back**. That is a real difference and it is `LITERATURE_REVIEW.md §5 Gap 3`.

**Citation.** Yu, W., Zhang, H., Pan, X., Cao, P., Ma, K., Li, J., Wang, H., & Yu, D. (2024). *EMNLP 2024*, p. 14679. DOI [10.18653/v1/2024.emnlp-main.813](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2024.emnlp-main.813) · 41 citations

### Problem
Two distinct failure modes: *"the reliability of the retrieved information is not always guaranteed, and the retrieval of irrelevant data can mislead the response generation"*; and *"standard RALMs frequently neglect their intrinsic knowledge due to the interference from retrieved information."* Desired behaviour: use intrinsic knowledge when retrieval is poor, and *"in the absence of both intrinsic and retrieved knowledge, opt to respond with 'unknown' to avoid hallucination."*

### Methodology
**CHAIN-OF-NOTE (CON)** generates *"sequential reading notes for each retrieved document,"* assessing each document's relevance before integrating anything. Two deployment modes: (a) prompting GPT-4 with CON; (b) distillation — *"we utilized GPT-4 to create 10K CON data, subsequently trained on LLaMa-2 7B model."*

Metrics: **EM** (normalised per Karpukhin et al.) and **F1** for open-domain QA; **Rejection Rate (RR)** for unanswerable/real-time questions. GPT-4 is scored with **Accuracy rather than EM**, because *"since GPT-4 is not directly trained on open-domain QA benchmarks, employing EM / F1 for evaluation is challenging."*

### Results
- **+7.9 EM** on fully noisy documents, averaged across three open-domain QA datasets.
- **+10.5 increase in rejection rate** for real-time questions beyond the pre-training knowledge scope.
- **+1.97 average EM** across all three datasets using **LLaMa-2** as backbone.
- **Table 4 (RealTimeQA, unknown robustness):** Retrieve-Read **EM 15.6 / F1 19.9 / RR 6.1** → + CHAIN-OF-NOTE **EM 15.7 / F1 20.3 / RR 13.0**. Note the RR **more than doubles** while EM/F1 barely move — the gain is almost entirely *knowing when to refuse*.
- GPT-4 with CON outperforms chain-of-thought prompting.
- Improvement *"varies depending on whether DPR successfully retrieves relevant documents."*

### Advantages
Explicit, measurable **refusal capability** — rare in this literature; distillation into a 7B model works; per-document notes are inherently interpretable; robustness gains under noisy retrieval are the largest reported effect.

### Disadvantages (their Limitations, verbatim)
*"One major limitation of the CHAIN-OF-NOTE (CON) approach is its increased inference cost due to the sequential generation of notes. While CON is beneficial for assessing the relevance and integrating external knowledge, it results in longer response times, which is problematic for time-sensitive applications. Moreover, the system's efficiency depends on the conciseness and relevance of the generated notes, which can fluctuate based on the complexity of the retrieved documents."*

Also: distillation requires GPT-4 access; the four benchmarks are not all named in-text; note quality is itself unverified LLM output.

### Datasets
**TriviaQA** and **RealTimeQA** named explicitly; three open-domain QA datasets for the main results plus a fourth for fine-tuning experiments. 10K GPT-4-generated CON training set. Models: GPT-4, LLaMa-2 7B, DPR.

## C2-09 · Ammann, Golde & Akbik (2025) — Question Decomposition for RAG ✅ FULL TEXT

**Citation.** Ammann, P., Golde, J., & Akbik, A. (2025). *ACL 2025: Student Research Workshop*, p. 501. Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin. DOI [10.18653/v1/2025.acl-srw.32](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.acl-srw.32) · 9 citations

### Problem
Multi-hop questions defeat standard RAG because *"relevant facts are often distributed across multiple documents rather than co-occurring in one source."* Semantic similarity to the whole question retrieves no single passage that answers it.

### Methodology
Three stages: **(i)** an LLM decomposes the query into sub-questions; **(ii)** passages retrieved per sub-question; **(iii)** *"the merged candidate pool is reranked."* A filtering step retains *"only passages that clearly address distinct aspects of the original question, improving precision in the final evidence set."*

Four configurations compared: **Naive RAG**, **QD** (decomposition only), **RR** (reranking only), **QD+RR** (both). Generation with **Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct** in bfloat16, temperature 0.8, nucleus sampling top-p 0.8. Metrics: **Hits@4, Hits@10, MAP@10, MRR@10** for retrieval; **F1, EM, precision, recall** plus supporting-fact and joint metrics for answers. Code released.

The authors are explicit about novelty: *"Although reranking itself is standard, we show that pairing an off-the-shelf cross-encoder reranker with LLM-driven question decomposition bridges the retrieval gap on multi-hop questions and provides a practical, drop-in enhancement, without any extra training or specialized indexing."*

### Results
**MultiHop-RAG (retrieval):**
- **QD alone:** +4.4 points Hits@4, +2.9 Hits@10.
- **RR alone:** +7.6 points Hits@4; *"substantially improves MAP@10 and MRR@10."*
- **QD+RR:** best overall — **87.2% Hits@10 and 0.635 MRR@10**.
- Against the dataset's published baseline (**74.7% Hits@10, 0.586 MRR@10**): *"our QD+RR thus improves Hits@10 by 16.5% and MRR@10 by 8.4%"* — **achieved "despite using a smaller embedding model."**
- MAP@10 rises to 0.322 with QD+RR vs 0.274 for RR alone, *"suggesting that reranking not only filters noise but leverages the broader context to prioritize relevant passages."*

**HotpotQA dev (Table 2):**

| System | F1 | P | R | EM |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Naive RAG | 31.3 | 33.1 | 31.2 | 25.4 |
| QD | 32.3 | 34.3 | 32.0 | 26.1 |
| RR | 32.9 | 35.0 | 32.7 | 26.4 |
| **QD+RR** | **35.0** | **37.1** | **34.8** | **28.1** |

Supporting-fact metrics: Naive 18.4/12.0/42.8 · QD 17.0/10.6/44.1 · RR **19.6**/**12.9**/44.9 · QD+RR 17.9/11.2/**46.8**. Joint: Naive 8.7/5.9/20.2 · QD 8.0/5.2/20.7 · RR **9.5**/**6.4**/21.4 · QD+RR 8.9/5.8/**23.1**.

Note the nuance: **QD+RR wins on precision (46.8 supporting-fact, 23.1 joint) but RR alone wins on supporting-fact EM/F1** — decomposition trades some exactness for coverage. Their summary: *"the former improves coverage, while the latter restores precision."*

**Ablation:** comparing sub-query count to gold evidence count, *"both Pearson and Spearman coefficients are near zero... indicating no correlation"* — the decomposer does not learn how many hops a question actually needs.

### Advantages
Large retrieval gains with **no training and no specialised indexing**; two public named benchmarks; genuinely careful about which component contributes what; unusually honest about its own novelty.

### Disadvantages (their Limitations, verbatim — all six)
1. **Single-hop and adverse cases.** *"Question decomposition can be counterproductive when the original query is already specific. In such cases, subqueries may introduce noise or distract from the original intent."*
2. **Prompt and model sensitivity.** *"The quality of subqueries is sensitive to both the prompt design and the underlying LLM."*
3. **Computational overhead.** *"Generating M subqueries and reranking M × k candidate passages substantially increases latency and GPU requirements."*
